subtopic_detail: Septic arthritis versus transient synovitis in the acutely limping preschool child
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 4-year-old boy in the emergency department. For two days he has refused to put any weight on his right leg, and his mother says he was off his food and hot to touch overnight. He had a runny nose that settled a fortnight ago.

He lies with the right hip flexed, abducted and externally rotated, and cries with any attempt at internal rotation. There is no rash and no other joint is involved. Ultrasound of the right hip shows a moderate effusion.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 148/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.9 C
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 14.9 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), C-reactive protein 78 mg/L (<5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 56 mm/h (<15), blood culture collected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Urgent orthopaedic referral for hip joint aspiration before antibiotics are started
options.rationale: He meets four of the four predictors used in Australian practice: non-weight bearing, temperature above 38.5 C, erythrocyte sedimentation rate above 40 mm/h and white cell count above 12 x10^9/L. Aspiration of the effusion under orthopaedic care secures the microbiological diagnosis, and taking it before antibiotics preserves culture yield. (Source: RCH CPG: Septic Arthritis)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis before any invasive intervention
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging answers a different question: it is used when osteomyelitis is suspected alongside or instead of joint infection, or when the effusion is not accessible. Here ultrasound has already shown drainable fluid and imaging only delays the diagnostic tap. (Source: RCH CPG: Septic Arthritis)

options.text: Start intravenous flucloxacillin now and repeat the inflammatory markers in 24 hours
options.rationale: Antibiotics before aspiration reduce the chance of isolating an organism from joint fluid, which matters because treatment runs for weeks and may need narrowing. Give the first dose immediately after the sample is taken, not before it. (Source: RCH CPG: Septic Arthritis)

options.text: Admit for observation on regular paracetamol and repeat the hip ultrasound tomorrow
options.rationale: Serial ultrasound cannot distinguish infected from reactive fluid, so a repeat scan will not change the decision it is being used to defer. Observation is reasonable only when the predictor count is low and the child is afebrile. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Limp)

options.text: Oral ibuprofen with orthopaedic review in 48 hours if he is still not weight bearing
options.rationale: This is the pathway for transient synovitis, which is afebrile with normal or near-normal inflammatory markers. A temperature of 38.9 C with a C-reactive protein of 78 mg/L places him in the high-probability band and a 48 hour delay risks irreversible cartilage damage. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Limp)

explanation.summary: A hip held in flexion, abduction and external rotation is the position of maximum capsular volume and is the joint's way of minimising pressure from an effusion. The Kocher predictors were derived to separate septic arthritis from transient synovitis, and the probability of infection climbs steeply as predictors accumulate rather than at any single cut-off. Ultrasound reliably detects an effusion but cannot characterise it, so the fluid must be sampled. Untreated septic arthritis of the hip destroys articular cartilage within days and can infarct the femoral head, which is why this sits alongside testicular torsion as a same-day surgical problem.
key_points: The four predictors are non-weight bearing, fever above 38.5 C, erythrocyte sedimentation rate above 40 mm/h and white cell count above 12 x10^9/L
Ultrasound confirms an effusion but never tells you whether it is infected
Blood cultures and joint fluid go before the first antibiotic dose wherever the delay is minutes rather than hours
Transient synovitis follows a viral illness, the child is afebrile and inflammatory markers are normal or marginal
Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest organism beyond the neonatal period in Australia
explanation.pearls: Kingella kingae is the leading cause of septic arthritis between 6 months and 4 years and grows poorly on solid media, so joint fluid should be inoculated directly into a paediatric blood culture bottle at the bedside rather than sent dry.

subtopic_detail: Choosing hip ultrasound or radiograph by age in late-presenting developmental dysplasia
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 6-month-old girl brought in by her father, who has noticed that her nappy is harder to fasten on one side and that one leg looks shorter when she lies on her back. She was born at term in the breech position and her newborn hip examination was recorded as normal.

On examination there is asymmetry of the thigh skin creases and limited abduction of the left hip to 50 degrees. The Ortolani and Barlow manoeuvres are both negative.

data_table.Examination: Left hip abduction limited to 50 degrees, asymmetric thigh creases, apparent left femoral shortening, Ortolani and Barlow negative, spine and lower limb neurology normal

lead_in: Which investigation is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Static and dynamic ultrasound of both hips performed by a paediatric sonographer
options.rationale: Ultrasound is the correct modality under 4.5 months, when the femoral head is still cartilaginous and acoustically transparent. At 6 months the ossific nucleus casts an acoustic shadow over the medial acetabulum and the study becomes unreliable. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.text: Computed tomography of the pelvis with three-dimensional acetabular reconstruction
options.rationale: Computed tomography delivers a substantial gonadal radiation dose to an infant and adds nothing to a plain film at the diagnostic stage. It has a narrow role in complex revision surgical planning. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of both hips under general anaesthesia within two weeks
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is reserved for assessing reduction after closed or open surgical treatment, not for making the initial diagnosis. It requires sedation or anaesthesia in this age group for no diagnostic gain over a plain film. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.text: Anteroposterior radiograph of the pelvis with the hips in the neutral position
options.rationale: Beyond about 4.5 months the femoral head ossifies and the cartilaginous landmarks that ultrasound depends on are obscured, so the plain radiograph becomes the investigation of choice. Acetabular index and the relationship of the ossific nucleus to Perkin's and Hilgenreiner's lines are assessed. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.text: Repeat clinical hip examination by the child health nurse at the 12-month check
options.rationale: Limited abduction with apparent femoral shortening after 3 months is the presentation of an established dislocation, and Ortolani and Barlow become negative precisely because the hip is no longer reducible. Waiting six months converts a closed reduction into an open one. (Source: RACGP: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip)
source_refs: RACGP: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

explanation.summary: Developmental dysplasia of the hip is a spectrum from mild acetabular shallowness to fixed dislocation, and the physical signs change as the child grows. In the newborn the unstable hip can be provoked in and out of the socket, which is what the Ortolani and Barlow manoeuvres detect; once the hip sits dislocated and the soft tissues contract, those tests fall silent and asymmetric abduction becomes the most sensitive sign. Breech presentation, female sex and a positive family history are the three risk factors that trigger imaging in Australia even when the examination is normal. A normal newborn check never excludes the diagnosis, because dysplasia can develop after birth.
key_points: Ultrasound is the modality under 4.5 months; the plain pelvic radiograph takes over after that
Limited abduction and apparent femoral shortening are the signs of an established dislocation
Negative Ortolani and Barlow in an older infant is reassuring only if abduction is full and symmetric
Breech presentation at or after 36 weeks, female sex and a first-degree family history warrant imaging regardless of examination
Later diagnosis means a higher chance of open reduction, femoral osteotomy and early degenerative disease
explanation.pearls: A Pavlik harness is effective up to about 6 months of age and carries a failure rate above 50% once the hip is dislocated and irreducible, which is why the Australian newborn risk-factor ultrasound is booked at 6 weeks rather than left to the routine checks.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip
RACGP: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

subtopic_detail: Topical versus oral antibiotic threshold in childhood impetigo
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 5-year-old girl whose mother reports three crusty yellow patches around her right nostril and upper lip that appeared four days ago and are slowly spreading outwards. Her older brother had something similar last month.

She is systemically well, eating normally and has been at school throughout. Examination shows three discrete lesions, the largest 15 mm across, with honey-coloured crust and no surrounding spreading erythema, warmth or induration. There is no lymphadenopathy and no other body site is affected.

data_table.Examination: Three crusted lesions on the right perinasal skin and upper lip, largest 15 mm, no cellulitic margin, no regional lymphadenopathy, remainder of skin clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic management?

options.text: Topical fusidic acid twice daily with school exclusion until all crusts have gone
options.rationale: Fusidic acid resistance in Australian Staphylococcus aureus isolates is high enough that it is no longer preferred, and exclusion runs only until 24 hours of treatment with lesions covered, not until healing. Both halves of this option are wrong. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Topical mupirocin 2% applied three times daily for five days after crust removal
options.rationale: Australian guidance reserves oral antibiotics for widespread or multiple-site disease, systemic symptoms or outbreak settings, and treats localised impetigo topically. Soaking and removing crust first is part of the treatment because it lets the ointment reach the colonised skin. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole twice daily for a three-day short course
options.rationale: This is the regimen used in remote Australian communities where impetigo is often extensive and where methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus is common, and it is an oral agent for the same reason that oral cefalexin is wrong here. The near-pair distinction is the burden of disease, not the organism. (Source: National Healthy Skin Guideline)

options.text: Oral cefalexin given four times daily for a seven-day course starting today
options.rationale: Oral therapy is indicated when lesions are numerous, spread across multiple body regions, or the child is systemically unwell, none of which applies here. Using it for three localised lesions adds gastrointestinal side effects and selection pressure without improving cure rates. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Topical hydrogen peroxide 1% cream applied twice daily until the crusting settles
options.rationale: Antiseptic creams are an option in some overseas guidance for very limited disease but are not the Australian recommendation, and evidence for cure is weaker than for topical antibiotics. They have a role in decolonisation adjuncts rather than as primary treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Impetigo is a superficial bacterial infection of the epidermis, most often caused by Staphylococcus aureus and less commonly Streptococcus pyogenes, and the two cannot be separated clinically. The management decision is driven almost entirely by extent rather than by organism, because topical therapy cannot reliably cover widespread disease and oral therapy is unnecessary for a few lesions. Crust is a reservoir of organisms and a barrier to topical penetration, so soaking it off with a warm damp cloth before each application materially improves cure. The public health dimension matters in Australian practice because untreated streptococcal skin infection is a driver of acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and contributes to the rheumatic heart disease burden in some communities.
key_points: Localised disease is treated topically; oral antibiotics are for multiple sites, extensive lesions or systemic symptoms
Remove crust by soaking before each topical application
Fusidic acid is avoided in Australia because of resistance rates
Children may return to school 24 hours after treatment starts if lesions are covered
Recurrent or extensive impetigo warrants a scabies examination and household screening
explanation.pearls: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis follows skin infection by 3 to 6 weeks rather than the 1 to 2 weeks that follows pharyngitis, so a child with cola-coloured urine one month after impetigo needs a blood pressure and urinalysis, not a throat swab.

subtopic_detail: Timing of diagnostic audiology after a refer result on newborn hearing screening
stem:
You are the paediatric resident reviewing a 3-week-old boy in the newborn follow-up clinic. He was born at 39 weeks after an uncomplicated pregnancy and went home on day two. The state newborn hearing screening program recorded a refer result in the left ear on both the initial automated screen and the repeat screen before discharge, with a pass in the right ear.

He is feeding and growing well, and his mother says he startles to the dog barking. Examination including the external ears and a search for craniofacial or neck anomalies is unremarkable, and there is no family history of childhood deafness.

data_table.Examination: Normal pinnae and patent canals bilaterally, no preauricular pits or tags, no neck sinuses, no dysmorphic features, weight on the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to ear nose and throat surgery for tympanometry and microsuction of the left ear
options.rationale: Tympanometry is unreliable in the first few months because the infant ear canal is compliant, and there is no otoscopic abnormality to suction. Surgical referral follows the audiological diagnosis rather than preceding it. (Source: RCH CPG: Hearing Loss)

options.text: Reassure the parents and rescreen with automated testing at the 6-week immunisations
options.rationale: Rescreening has already been done and failed, so repeating the same test answers nothing and consumes the diagnostic window. A behavioural startle to a loud noise is a brainstem reflex that is preserved in unilateral and in moderate bilateral loss. (Source: Australian Newborn Hearing Screening Framework)

options.text: Refer for diagnostic auditory brainstem response testing to be completed by 3 months
options.rationale: A refer result that persists on the repeat screen triggers diagnostic audiological assessment, and the Australian benchmark is diagnosis by 3 months with intervention started by 6 months. Diagnostic auditory brainstem response gives ear-specific and frequency-specific thresholds that the automated screen cannot. (Source: Australian Newborn Hearing Screening Framework)

options.text: Arrange congenital cytomegalovirus urine testing and defer audiology until that returns
options.rationale: Urine polymerase chain reaction for cytomegalovirus is genuinely time-critical and should be collected within the first 3 weeks, so it is done in parallel rather than instead of audiology. Sequencing it ahead of the hearing assessment delays both. (Source: RCH CPG: Hearing Loss)

options.text: Arrange developmental surveillance with formal speech assessment at 12 months of age
options.rationale: Waiting for speech delay to declare itself is the historical pathway that universal newborn screening was built to replace, since language outcomes deteriorate sharply once amplification starts after 6 months. Surveillance supplements audiology but cannot substitute for it. (Source: Australian Newborn Hearing Screening Framework)

explanation.summary: Universal newborn hearing screening in Australia uses automated auditory brainstem response or otoacoustic emissions to sort infants into pass and refer, and a refer result is a screening flag rather than a diagnosis. The purpose of the programme is captured in the 1-3-6 framework: screen by 1 month, diagnose by 3 months and start intervention by 6 months, because receptive and expressive language outcomes track closely with the age at which amplification begins. Unilateral loss still matters, producing difficulty with sound localisation and with speech discrimination in noisy classrooms. Congenital cytomegalovirus is the commonest non-genetic cause and is only diagnosable from a sample taken in the first three weeks, after which a positive result cannot be distinguished from postnatal acquisition.
key_points: A refer result on the repeat screen leads to diagnostic audiology, not to another screen
The Australian benchmark is diagnosis by 3 months and intervention by 6 months
A startle response does not exclude significant hearing loss
Congenital cytomegalovirus testing must be collected within the first 3 weeks of life
Unilateral loss requires follow-up because of localisation and speech-in-noise difficulty
explanation.pearls: Congenital cytomegalovirus hearing loss can be progressive and late onset, so an infant with a positive urine polymerase chain reaction needs audiological review every 6 months to at least 3 years even if the initial diagnostic assessment shows normal thresholds.

subtopic_detail: Separating true infantile esotropia from pseudostrabismus on cover testing
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 7-month-old girl whose grandmother is convinced that her left eye turns inwards, particularly in photographs. Her mother has not noticed it and says the baby looks at her normally during feeds.

The baby has a broad flat nasal bridge and prominent skin folds at the inner corners of both eyes. The corneal light reflex is displaced laterally in the left eye. On cover testing, covering the right eye produces an outward movement of the left eye to take up fixation. She was born at term and her development is age appropriate.

data_table.Examination: Prominent bilateral epicanthic folds, corneal light reflex displaced temporally in the left eye, cover test shows outward refixation movement of the left eye, red reflex present and symmetric bilaterally

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to a paediatric ophthalmologist for assessment within the next few weeks
options.rationale: An abnormal cover test with a refixation movement confirms a manifest deviation and excludes pseudostrabismus, whatever the epicanthic folds suggest. Any constant squint beyond 3 to 4 months of age needs specialist assessment because amblyopia develops rapidly in the sensitive period. (Source: RCH CPG: Squint)

options.text: Commence part-time occlusion of the right eye with patching for two hours each day
options.rationale: Occlusion therapy treats amblyopia once refraction and visual acuity have been measured and the deviation characterised, and the amount of patching is titrated to those findings. Starting it in general practice risks treating the wrong eye or over-occluding. (Source: RANZCO: Paediatric Vision Screening)

options.text: Arrange urgent ocular ultrasound to exclude an intraocular mass before any referral
options.rationale: Squint can be the presenting sign of retinoblastoma, but the screening test for that is the red reflex, which is present and symmetric here. Ordering imaging ahead of an ophthalmological examination inverts the assessment sequence. (Source: RCH CPG: Squint)

options.text: Refer to an optometrist for cycloplegic refraction and spectacle correction if needed
options.rationale: Cycloplegic refraction is an essential part of the workup because accommodative esotropia responds to hypermetropic correction, but an infant with a constant deviation needs the full orthoptic and ophthalmological assessment that includes it. This option covers only one component. (Source: RANZCO: Paediatric Vision Screening)

options.text: Reassure that this is pseudostrabismus from the epicanthic folds and review in 6 months
options.rationale: Pseudostrabismus is the correct label only when the corneal light reflexes are symmetric and the cover test shows no refixation movement, because the folds merely obscure nasal sclera. Here both tests are abnormal, so the appearance is real. (Source: RCH CPG: Squint)

explanation.summary: Strabismus in infancy is common enough that the clinical task is separating a true deviation from the far more frequent pseudostrabismus produced by a broad nasal bridge and epicanthic folds. Two bedside tests settle it: the corneal light reflex should sit symmetrically just nasal to the centre of each pupil, and the cover test should produce no movement in the uncovered eye if both eyes are already fixing. Intermittent deviation before 3 to 4 months can be physiological as binocular control matures, but a constant deviation at any age and any deviation beyond 4 months is pathological. The clinical stake is amblyopia, where the cortex suppresses input from the deviating eye and visual development is permanently curtailed if not treated within the sensitive period.
key_points: Symmetric corneal light reflexes plus a normal cover test defines pseudostrabismus
A refixation movement on cover testing means a true manifest deviation
Any constant squint, or any squint after 4 months of age, needs ophthalmology referral
Always check the red reflex, because leukocoria may signal retinoblastoma or cataract
Amblyopia treatment is far more effective before 7 years of age
explanation.pearls: Accommodative esotropia typically appears between 2 and 3 years in a hypermetropic child and can be fully corrected by glasses alone, so cycloplegic refraction precedes any discussion of squint surgery.

subtopic_detail: Slit lamp surveillance interval for silent uveitis in antinuclear antibody positive oligoarticular arthritis
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the rheumatology clinic reviewing a 3-year-old girl diagnosed six weeks ago with arthritis of the right knee and left ankle, persisting for four months with no other joints involved. She has no fever, no rash and no systemic features.

Her parents report that her eyes have never been red, sore or watery and that she does not avoid bright light. Antinuclear antibody is positive at a titre of 1:320 and rheumatoid factor is negative. Intra-articular corticosteroid injections are planned and her arthritis is otherwise well controlled on naproxen.

data_table.Examination: Synovitis of the right knee and left ankle with 10 degree fixed flexion at the knee, no rash, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, white eyes with normal pupils and visual behaviour
data_table.Investigations: Antinuclear antibody positive 1:320, rheumatoid factor negative, C-reactive protein 6 mg/L (<5), haemoglobin 118 g/L (110-140)

lead_in: What ophthalmological follow-up should be arranged?

options.text: Slit lamp examination every 3 months, continuing for several years from diagnosis
options.rationale: Antinuclear antibody positivity, oligoarticular subtype, female sex and onset under 7 years together define the highest risk group for chronic anterior uveitis, which is screened 3-monthly. The interval is short because the inflammation is asymptomatic and white-eyed until structural damage has occurred. (Source: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: JIA Uveitis Screening)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: JIA Uveitis Screening

options.text: Ophthalmology review only if her eyes become red, painful or sensitive to bright light
options.rationale: This inverts the central fact about this complication: the uveitis of oligoarticular arthritis is characteristically painless and the eye stays white, unlike the acute anterior uveitis of the spondyloarthropathies. Symptom-triggered review means presentation at the stage of band keratopathy or cataract. (Source: RCH CPG: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis)

options.text: Fundoscopy every 3 months performed in the rheumatology clinic by the treating team
options.rationale: The pathology is in the anterior chamber, which direct fundoscopy does not visualise, and the near-pair distinction from the correct answer is the instrument rather than the interval. Screening must be done on a slit lamp by someone trained to grade anterior chamber activity. (Source: RCH CPG: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis)

options.text: Visual acuity testing every 3 months by the orthoptist with slit lamp only if reduced
options.rationale: Acuity is preserved until the anterior chamber inflammation has caused posterior synechiae, cataract or glaucoma, so it is a late and insensitive marker. Only the slit lamp detects the cells and flare that define active disease. (Source: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: JIA Uveitis Screening)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: JIA Uveitis Screening

options.text: Slit lamp examination every 12 months, continuing for several years from diagnosis
options.rationale: Annual screening is the interval used for the low-risk groups, such as antinuclear antibody negative children with polyarticular disease or those with systemic onset arthritis. Applying it to this risk profile misses the window in which silent inflammation can be caught. (Source: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: JIA Uveitis Screening)
source_refs: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: JIA Uveitis Screening

explanation.summary: Chronic anterior uveitis complicates juvenile idiopathic arthritis in a pattern almost perfectly inverse to the joint disease: the children with the fewest joints involved and the mildest arthritis carry the highest ocular risk. The inflammation runs entirely independently of joint activity, so a child whose arthritis is in remission is not thereby protected and screening continues regardless. Because the eye remains white and the child never complains, the diagnosis is made only by planned slit lamp examination, and the complications that follow missed disease are posterior synechiae, band keratopathy, cataract, glaucoma and permanent vision loss. Risk stratification in Australian practice is built from antinuclear antibody status, arthritis subtype and age at onset, and it sets the screening interval rather than whether screening happens at all.
key_points: Highest risk is antinuclear antibody positive, oligoarticular onset, young and female
Screening for the high-risk group is 3-monthly slit lamp examination
The uveitis is painless with a white eye and normal acuity until late
Ocular inflammation is independent of joint disease activity and of treatment response
Systemic onset juvenile idiopathic arthritis carries the lowest uveitis risk
explanation.pearls: Methotrexate reduces the incidence of uveitis flares in juvenile idiopathic arthritis, and adalimumab added to methotrexate is the escalation for refractory disease, but neither alters the screening interval while the child remains in the high-risk category.

sources.label: Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group: JIA Uveitis Screening

subtopic_detail: Imaging acute haematogenous bone infection when the plain radiograph is still normal
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar assessing a 9-year-old boy with five days of increasing pain in the left lower thigh and two days of fever. His mother says he has been limping and will not run, and that he grazed the same knee playing football a fortnight ago. The graze has healed.

He is tender to firm pressure over the distal femoral metaphysis with no overlying warmth or fluctuance. The knee itself has a full painless range of movement and no effusion on ultrasound. A radiograph of the femur shows only subtle soft tissue swelling with no periosteal reaction or lytic change.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118/min, blood pressure 104/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.6 C
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 15.8 x10^9/L (4.5-13.5), C-reactive protein 96 mg/L (<5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 64 mm/h (<15), blood cultures collected, femoral radiograph shows soft tissue swelling only

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat plain radiograph of the femur in 10 days to look for new periosteal reaction
options.rationale: Serial films will eventually become positive, which is exactly the problem: waiting for radiographic change means treating a 2-week-old infection that has had time to form sequestrum. The test is specific but far too slow for this decision. (Source: RCH CPG: Osteomyelitis)

options.text: Computed tomography of the femur with reconstruction to assess the cortex and marrow
options.rationale: Computed tomography shows cortical destruction and sequestrum well, which makes it useful in chronic osteomyelitis, but it is relatively insensitive to the marrow oedema of early disease. The near-pair distinction from magnetic resonance imaging is that one images mineral and the other images marrow water. (Source: RCH CPG: Osteomyelitis)

options.text: Technetium-99m bone scan of the whole skeleton, arranged as an inpatient this week
options.rationale: Bone scintigraphy is sensitive early and retains a role when the site is unclear or multifocal disease is suspected, but it gives poor anatomical resolution and cannot show a drainable collection. It is the fallback when magnetic resonance imaging is unavailable or the child cannot be scanned. (Source: RCH CPG: Osteomyelitis)

options.text: Ultrasound of the distal femur to look for a subperiosteal collection and guide aspiration
options.rationale: Ultrasound can demonstrate subperiosteal pus and periosteal elevation once those have developed, and it is useful for guiding aspiration, but a negative study does not exclude intramedullary infection. It cannot see into the marrow, which is where the disease starts. (Source: RCH CPG: Osteomyelitis)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the femur with contrast, arranged as an inpatient today
options.rationale: Plain films stay normal for 10 to 14 days because roughly a third of bone mineral must be lost before lysis is visible, so a normal radiograph at day 5 carries no reassurance. Magnetic resonance imaging detects the marrow oedema of early infection and defines any subperiosteal or intraosseous collection that would need surgical drainage. (Source: RCH CPG: Osteomyelitis)

explanation.summary: Acute haematogenous osteomyelitis in children seeds the metaphysis, where sluggish flow in the vascular loops adjacent to the physis favours bacterial lodgement, and it is therefore metaphyseal tenderness rather than joint signs that localises the disease. The trap in this presentation is that the adjacent joint is normal, so a limp with fever can be wrongly attributed to a musculoskeletal strain when the radiograph comes back clear. Staphylococcus aureus dominates, and empirical therapy in Australia is high-dose intravenous flucloxacillin with the duration guided by clinical and C-reactive protein response before an oral switch. Surgery is required when there is a subperiosteal or intraosseous collection, when the child fails to respond to antibiotics, or when there is an adjacent septic joint.
key_points: Plain radiographs remain normal for 10 to 14 days and cannot exclude early osteomyelitis
Magnetic resonance imaging shows marrow oedema early and identifies drainable collections
Metaphyseal tenderness with a normal adjacent joint is the characteristic localising sign
Staphylococcus aureus is the dominant pathogen beyond the neonatal period
Blood cultures are positive in a substantial minority and may be the only microbiological yield
explanation.pearls: In the hip, shoulder and elbow the metaphysis lies inside the joint capsule, so metaphyseal osteomyelitis at those three sites can decompress directly into the joint and produce a concurrent septic arthritis that changes the operation required.

subtopic_detail: Gonadotrophin stimulation to separate central from peripheral early puberty in a girl under eight
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 6-year-old girl referred because her mother noticed breast development four months ago that has continued to progress. She has also grown out of two shoe sizes this year and has developed body odour, but there is no pubic or axillary hair.

She has no headaches, no visual symptoms and no history of central nervous system insult. There are no cafe-au-lait patches and the abdominal examination is normal. Her height has crossed from the 50th to the 90th centile over 18 months, and a bone age radiograph reads 9 years against a chronological age of 6 years.

data_table.Examination: Breast Tanner stage 3, pubic hair Tanner stage 1, no axillary hair, no cafe-au-lait macules, no abdominal mass, fundi normal, visual fields full to confrontation
data_table.Investigations: Bone age 9 years at chronological age 6 years, oestradiol detectable, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, early morning basal luteinising hormone equivocal

lead_in: Which investigation will best clarify the underlying mechanism?

options.text: Gonadotrophin releasing hormone stimulation test with serial luteinising hormone sampling
options.rationale: A pubertal luteinising hormone rise after stimulation proves that the hypothalamic pituitary gonadal axis has been reactivated, which is the definition of central precocious puberty and the trigger for brain imaging and for treatment. An equivocal basal level cannot make that distinction, which is why the dynamic test exists. (Source: APEG: Precocious Puberty)

options.text: Pelvic ultrasound measuring uterine length and assessing both ovaries for a mass lesion
options.rationale: Pelvic ultrasound is a useful adjunct that shows oestrogen exposure and can reveal an autonomous ovarian cyst or tumour, but uterine changes reflect oestrogen from any source. It describes the downstream effect rather than identifying whether the drive is central. (Source: APEG: Precocious Puberty)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and pituitary with dedicated hypothalamic views
options.rationale: Brain imaging is the right next step once central precocious puberty has been confirmed, particularly in a girl this young where the yield for hypothalamic hamartoma and other lesions is meaningful. Ordering it before the axis has been characterised images children whose problem is peripheral. (Source: APEG: Precocious Puberty)

options.text: Serum beta human chorionic gonadotrophin with alpha fetoprotein and a repeat oestradiol
options.rationale: Germ cell tumour markers matter in boys with peripheral precocity, where beta human chorionic gonadotrophin can drive testicular testosterone production, and have little role in an isolated female thelarche. They are a reasonable adjunct but will not answer the central versus peripheral question. (Source: APEG: Precocious Puberty)

options.text: Serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone with androstenedione and an early morning cortisol level
options.rationale: This panel investigates adrenal androgen excess, which produces pubic and axillary hair, acne and clitoromegaly rather than breast development. The isolated thelarche with Tanner stage 1 pubic hair points away from an adrenal source. (Source: APEG: Precocious Puberty)

explanation.summary: Precocious puberty is defined in Australian practice as secondary sexual development before 8 years in girls and before 9 years in boys, and the first branch point is whether the hypothalamic pituitary gonadal axis has switched on early or whether sex steroids are arriving from an autonomous peripheral source. Central disease is gonadotrophin dependent and follows the normal sequence of puberty, whereas peripheral causes such as an ovarian cyst, an adrenal tumour or McCune-Albright syndrome produce a disordered sequence with suppressed gonadotrophins. Bone age advancement matters because premature epiphyseal fusion is what costs final adult height, and it is the main reason to treat. Isolated premature thelarche without growth acceleration or bone age advance is a benign non-progressive variant that needs observation rather than a workup of this depth.
key_points: Central precocious puberty is gonadotrophin dependent and confirmed by a pubertal luteinising hormone response to stimulation
Peripheral precocity has suppressed gonadotrophins and a disordered pubertal sequence
Bone age advancement and growth acceleration separate progressive disease from benign thelarche
Brain imaging follows confirmation of central disease and has a higher yield the younger the child
Treatment of central disease is with a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist to preserve adult height
explanation.pearls: A gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist such as leuprorelin paradoxically suppresses the axis by continuous rather than pulsatile receptor stimulation, and treatment is generally continued until around 11 years of bone age to maximise the adult height gained.

subtopic_detail: Interpreting coeliac serology taken after gluten has already been withdrawn from the diet
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing an 8-year-old girl whose parents removed wheat from her diet three months ago because of bloating and loose stools, with good symptomatic improvement. They now want the diagnosis confirmed.

Her weight has tracked along the 10th centile and her height along the 25th, both unchanged over two years. Her mother has autoimmune thyroid disease. Blood taken last week shows a tissue transglutaminase IgA of 3 U/mL with a total IgA within the normal range, and a normal full blood count with ferritin 34 micrograms/L (15-200).

data_table.Examination: Weight on the 10th centile, height on the 25th centile, abdomen soft and non-tender, no clubbing, no mouth ulcers, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Tissue transglutaminase IgA 3 U/mL (<15), total IgA within normal limits, haemoglobin 126 g/L (115-155), ferritin 34 micrograms/L (15-200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the family that coeliac disease is excluded and continue the gluten free diet
options.rationale: This is the central trap: the serology was taken under conditions that make a negative result uninformative rather than reassuring. Committing a child to a lifelong restrictive diet without a diagnosis also removes her access to follow-up, bone density surveillance and family screening. (Source: GESA: Coeliac Disease Clinical Update)

options.text: Request HLA DQ2 and DQ8 typing and stop further investigation if both come back positive
options.rationale: Human leucocyte antigen typing is valuable only for its negative predictive value, because a negative result effectively excludes coeliac disease for life, and it is unaffected by diet. A positive result is shared by roughly a third of the population and confirms nothing. (Source: GESA: Coeliac Disease Clinical Update)

options.text: Request deamidated gliadin peptide IgG antibodies to improve the sensitivity of testing
options.rationale: Deamidated gliadin peptide testing is genuinely useful when total IgA is deficient, since it is an IgG-based assay, but total IgA is normal here. It is subject to exactly the same normalisation on a gluten free diet as tissue transglutaminase, so it does not solve the problem. (Source: GESA: Coeliac Disease Clinical Update)

options.text: Refer for upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with duodenal biopsies on her current diet
options.rationale: Villous architecture recovers on a gluten free diet just as serology does, so biopsies taken now risk a false negative and an unnecessary anaesthetic. Endoscopy has a place after the challenge if the repeat serology is positive or discordant. (Source: GESA: Coeliac Disease Clinical Update)

options.text: Reintroduce gluten for at least six weeks and then repeat the tissue transglutaminase IgA
options.rationale: Coeliac serology measures an immune response to ingested gluten and normalises within weeks to months of withdrawal, so a negative result on a gluten-restricted diet cannot exclude the diagnosis. An adequate gluten challenge before retesting is the only way to make the result interpretable. (Source: GESA: Coeliac Disease Clinical Update)

explanation.summary: The commonest avoidable error in coeliac diagnosis is testing a patient who has already started a gluten free diet, because both the serological and the histological abnormalities are consequences of ongoing gluten exposure and both resolve without it. An adequate challenge means a meaningful daily gluten intake for at least six weeks in children before serology is repeated, and longer if biopsy is planned. Securing the diagnosis matters more than the symptom response suggests, because it drives long-term surveillance for iron and bone mineral deficiency, first-degree relative screening, and the distinction from non-coeliac gluten sensitivity, which needs no lifelong restriction. Human leucocyte antigen typing sits outside the diet problem entirely and is best used when a challenge is refused or poorly tolerated, since a negative result closes the question permanently.
key_points: Coeliac serology and duodenal histology both normalise on a gluten free diet
A gluten challenge of at least six weeks is needed before repeat testing in a child
Total IgA must accompany tissue transglutaminase IgA because selective IgA deficiency causes false negatives
HLA DQ2 and DQ8 typing is diet independent and useful for its negative predictive value only
Confirming the diagnosis triggers family screening and long-term nutritional surveillance
explanation.pearls: Selective IgA deficiency is about ten times more common in coeliac disease than in the general population, so an undetectable tissue transglutaminase IgA with a low total IgA should be followed by an IgG-based assay rather than read as a negative result.

subtopic_detail: Adding oral ivermectin to topical therapy for hyperkeratotic crusted scabies in a child
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar at a regional hospital admitting a 7-year-old Aboriginal boy flown in from a remote community with thick, scaly, fissured plaques over his hands, feet, elbows and scalp that have built up over several months. His grandmother says the whole family has had itchy skin, and that his skin has been getting crustier despite two courses of a cream from the clinic.

He has widespread hyperkeratotic crusting with underlying erythema and several fissures that are weeping. He is afebrile with no cellulitic margin. Skin scrapings show numerous mites and eggs. He has no history of immunosuppression and his weight is 22 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96/min, blood pressure 100/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 C
data_table.Examination: Thick hyperkeratotic plaques on hands, feet, elbows and scalp with fissuring, no spreading erythema or warmth, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Skin scrapings show numerous mites and eggs, white cell count 9.8 x10^9/L (4.5-13.5), C-reactive protein 8 mg/L (<5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment regimen?

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin for secondary infection followed by topical permethrin on discharge
options.rationale: Bacterial superinfection is a genuine and serious complication of this condition, but he is afebrile with normal inflammatory markers and no cellulitic margin, so there is nothing to treat today. Deferring definitive scabicide until discharge leaves the mite burden untouched. (Source: National Healthy Skin Guideline)

options.text: Topical permethrin 5% applied on two occasions one week apart with household treatment
options.rationale: This is the correct regimen for ordinary scabies and is precisely what has already failed twice, because the cream cannot penetrate hyperkeratotic crust to reach the mites beneath it. Treating the household remains essential but is not sufficient for the index case. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral ivermectin in repeated doses combined with topical permethrin and a keratolytic agent
options.rationale: The crusted form carries a mite burden orders of magnitude above ordinary scabies, and the hyperkeratosis physically shields mites from topical agents, so neither modality succeeds alone. Australian guidance combines repeated oral ivermectin with topical scabicide and a keratolytic to break down the crust, with the number of doses set by disease grade. (Source: National Healthy Skin Guideline)

options.text: Topical benzyl benzoate applied daily for one week with oral antihistamines for itching
options.rationale: Benzyl benzoate is an alternative scabicide but is irritant on fissured skin and remains a topical agent facing the same penetration barrier. Antihistamines address the symptom of itch without reducing the mite load that is driving it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral ivermectin as a single weight-based dose with review in the outpatient clinic weekly
options.rationale: A single dose does not cover eggs that hatch after treatment, and in the crusted form even the standard two-dose schedule is inadequate. The near-pair distinction from the correct answer is the number of doses and the absence of the topical and keratolytic components. (Source: National Healthy Skin Guideline)

explanation.summary: Crusted scabies represents a failed host response to Sarcoptes scabiei, with mite numbers in the thousands to millions rather than the ten or so carried in ordinary infestation, and it is correspondingly far more contagious. It is classically associated with immunosuppression but occurs in people with no identifiable immune defect, and in Australia it is concentrated in remote communities where it drives ongoing transmission, recurrent skin infection and the downstream burden of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and rheumatic heart disease. Grading by crusting distribution, thickness and skin condition determines how many ivermectin doses are given. Because the index case seeds the household and the wider community, treating contacts simultaneously is part of the treatment rather than an optional public health add-on.
key_points: Crusted scabies carries a vastly higher mite burden and is far more transmissible than ordinary scabies
Hyperkeratotic crust blocks topical penetration, so combined oral and topical therapy is required
Keratolytic treatment softens crust and lets the scabicide reach the mites
Ivermectin dose number is set by disease grade rather than being fixed
Simultaneous treatment of household and close contacts prevents immediate reinfestation
explanation.pearls: Itch persists for 2 to 4 weeks after successful scabies treatment because it is a hypersensitivity response to retained mite antigen, so ongoing scratching in that window should prompt a moisturiser and a topical corticosteroid rather than a third course of scabicide.

subtopic_detail: Murmur characteristics that mandate echocardiography in an otherwise well school-aged child
stem:
You are the general practitioner performing a pre-participation check on a 10-year-old boy before he joins a representative football squad. He has no symptoms, exercises without breathlessness and has never fainted. There is no family history of sudden cardiac death or inherited heart disease.

He is well grown with normal femoral pulses and no cyanosis or clubbing. Auscultation reveals a soft early diastolic murmur heard best at the left sternal edge in the third intercostal space, unchanged when he sits forward, with a normal first and second heart sound and no thrill.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76/min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg in the right arm, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Soft early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge, no thrill, normal first and second heart sounds, femoral pulses present and synchronous with radial, no hepatomegaly

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange serial blood pressure measurement in all four limbs and review the findings in a month
options.rationale: Four-limb blood pressures are aimed at coarctation of the aorta, which produces radiofemoral delay and diminished femoral pulses, and his femoral pulses are present and synchronous. This investigates a different lesion from the one the auscultatory findings indicate. (Source: RCH CPG: Heart Murmurs)

options.text: Reassure and review in 12 months, as this has the features of a Still's vibratory murmur
options.rationale: A Still's murmur is a low-pitched vibratory mid-systolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge that softens on standing, and it is the commonest innocent murmur at this age. The near-pair distinction is timing: Still's is systolic, and this murmur is not. (Source: RCH CPG: Heart Murmurs)

options.text: Reassure and review in 12 months, as the murmur has all the features of a venous hum
options.rationale: A venous hum is continuous rather than confined to diastole, is loudest in the neck and infraclavicular area, and characteristically disappears when the child lies flat or the neck veins are compressed. None of those features is present. (Source: RCH CPG: Heart Murmurs)

options.text: Arrange an electrocardiogram and chest radiograph and refer only if either is abnormal
options.rationale: Both tests are insensitive for the valve lesions that produce a diastolic murmur, and a normal electrocardiogram with a normal chest film would not exclude aortic regurgitation. Using them as a gate to referral risks a falsely reassuring result. (Source: RCH CPG: Heart Murmurs)

options.text: Refer for echocardiography and paediatric cardiology assessment before clearing him to play
options.rationale: Any diastolic murmur is pathological regardless of how soft it is or how well the child appears, because normal flow across normal valves does not generate diastolic turbulence. Innocent murmur criteria apply only to systolic murmurs, so no combination of reassuring features rescues this one. (Source: RCH CPG: Heart Murmurs)

explanation.summary: Murmurs are audible in a large proportion of healthy children at some point, and the clinical skill is applying the criteria that define an innocent murmur rather than relying on the absence of symptoms. Innocent murmurs are soft, systolic, short, sited over a small area, unaccompanied by a thrill, and vary with posture, with normal heart sounds and normal pulses. Diastolic timing sits outside that framework entirely: it reflects either regurgitation through a semilunar valve or turbulent flow across an atrioventricular valve, both of which are structural. In an athletic pre-participation context the decision carries additional weight because clearing a child with an undiagnosed structural lesion for competitive sport transfers the risk to an unsupervised setting.
key_points: Every diastolic murmur is pathological and requires echocardiography
Innocent murmur criteria apply only to systolic murmurs
A Still's murmur is vibratory, mid-systolic, at the lower left sternal edge and softens on standing
A venous hum is continuous, loudest above the clavicle, and abolished by lying flat
Absent or delayed femoral pulses point to coarctation and need four-limb blood pressures
explanation.pearls: In Australian children an early diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation or a mid-diastolic mitral murmur should prompt consideration of rheumatic heart disease, which remains a leading cause of acquired valve disease in young people in northern and central Australia and is diagnosed echocardiographically.

sources.label: RHD Australia: Guideline for Rheumatic Heart Disease

subtopic_detail: Referred knee pain with a normal anteroposterior hip film in an adolescent with a high body mass index
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 12-year-old boy with six weeks of aching in the left knee, worse after sport and better with rest, which his father attributes to a growth spurt. There was no injury. For the past week he has been walking with his left foot turned outwards.

He is afebrile and systemically well. The left knee has a full range of movement, no effusion, no joint line tenderness and no ligamentous laxity. When the left hip is flexed it rolls into external rotation, and internal rotation is limited to 10 degrees. His body mass index is on the 97th centile. An anteroposterior radiograph of the pelvis is reported by the emergency consultant as showing no fracture and no joint space loss.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82/min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Left knee examination normal, obligatory external rotation on left hip flexion, left hip internal rotation limited to 10 degrees, left leg externally rotated on standing, no thigh or calf tenderness
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 3 mg/L (<5), white cell count 7.4 x10^9/L (4.5-13.5), anteroposterior pelvic radiograph reported as showing no fracture

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Make him non-weight bearing and obtain frog-leg lateral views of both hips urgently
options.rationale: Early slippage displaces the femoral epiphysis posteriorly, which an anteroposterior projection can miss entirely while the lateral view shows it clearly, so a normal single-view film does not exclude the diagnosis. Weight bearing risks converting a stable slip into an unstable one, which carries a far higher rate of avascular necrosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Upper Femoral Epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Upper Femoral Epiphysis

options.text: Arrange outpatient magnetic resonance imaging of the left knee within the next two weeks
options.rationale: The knee examination is entirely normal and the abnormal findings are all at the hip, so imaging the symptomatic site rather than the pathological one is the classic error in this presentation. Allowing him to walk for two weeks meanwhile is the more serious half of the mistake. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Upper Femoral Epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Upper Femoral Epiphysis

options.text: Request an ultrasound of the left hip to look for an effusion suggesting joint infection
options.rationale: He is afebrile with a C-reactive protein of 3 mg/L and a normal white cell count, which makes septic arthritis very unlikely, and the six-week history is wrong for it. Ultrasound may show a small effusion in this condition but does not visualise the epiphyseal displacement that defines it. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Limp)

options.text: Discharge with simple analgesia, activity modification and general practitioner review in a month
options.rationale: Obligatory external rotation on hip flexion with restricted internal rotation is a specific mechanical sign that cannot be explained by growth-related knee pain. Progression during a month of continued weight bearing is what turns a pinning operation into a salvage one. (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Limp)

options.text: Request thyroid function tests and a bone profile before arranging any further hip imaging
options.rationale: Endocrinopathy including hypothyroidism and renal osteodystrophy is a genuine association worth screening for, particularly in atypical age groups or bilateral disease, but it is a parallel investigation rather than a prerequisite. Sequencing it first delays the imaging that determines today's management. (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Upper Femoral Epiphysis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Upper Femoral Epiphysis

explanation.summary: Hip pathology refers pain along the obturator nerve distribution to the medial thigh and knee, so a child presenting with knee pain and a normal knee examination has a hip problem until proven otherwise. Slipped upper femoral epiphysis occurs during the adolescent growth spurt when shear forces across a widened physis exceed its strength, and obesity is the dominant risk factor in Australian practice. The physical sign that gives it away is obligatory external rotation as the hip is flexed, produced by the posteriorly displaced epiphysis. The stakes are set by two complications, avascular necrosis and chondrolysis, both of which rise sharply if a stable slip is allowed to become unstable, which is why non-weight bearing begins before the confirmatory image is obtained rather than after it.
key_points: Knee pain with a normal knee examination requires a full hip assessment
The anteroposterior view alone can miss early posterior slippage; a lateral view is mandatory
Obligatory external rotation on hip flexion is the characteristic mechanical sign
Make the child non-weight bearing immediately, before imaging confirms the diagnosis
Avascular necrosis risk is much higher in unstable than in stable slips
explanation.pearls: Around one in five slips is bilateral at presentation and a further proportion of the remainder slip on the other side within 18 months, so both hips are imaged at diagnosis and the contralateral side is reviewed at every follow-up until the physes close.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Slipped Upper Femoral Epiphysis

subtopic_detail: Marrow examination before corticosteroids when arthritis is accompanied by disproportionate night pain
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 5-year-old girl referred with eight weeks of joint pain and swelling affecting both knees and the left wrist. She has had intermittent fevers to 38.2 C and has become reluctant to walk in the mornings.

Her parents describe her waking crying at night with pain in her shins that settles with cuddling, and say she has stopped wanting to be picked up under the arms. Examination confirms synovitis of both knees. She has no rash and no lymphadenopathy, and her liver and spleen are not enlarged. The rheumatology consultant is considering starting oral prednisolone while awaiting the antinuclear antibody result.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.8 C
data_table.Examination: Synovitis of both knees and the left wrist, tenderness over both tibial shafts away from any joint, no rash, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 92 g/L (115-135), white cell count 4.1 x10^9/L (4.5-13.5), neutrophils 1.6 x10^9/L (1.5-8.0), platelets 108 x10^9/L (150-400), C-reactive protein 42 mg/L (<5), lactate dehydrogenase raised, blood film not yet examined

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start oral prednisolone for presumed systemic arthritis and review the response in one week
options.rationale: This is the specific error the presentation is built around, because a partial response to steroid is common in marrow disease and provides false reassurance. Systemic onset arthritis also typically raises rather than lowers the white cell count and platelet count. (Source: RCH CPG: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis)

options.text: Start naproxen and repeat the full blood count with inflammatory markers in two weeks
options.rationale: A non-steroidal agent is a reasonable holding treatment in uncomplicated arthritis and avoids the steroid problem, but a two-week delay is unacceptable when the counts already show bicytopenia. The safety of the drug does not compensate for the delay in diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Leukaemia)

options.text: Discuss urgently with haematology and arrange bone marrow examination before any corticosteroid
options.rationale: Two or more reduced cell lines with severe non-articular bone pain and a raised lactate dehydrogenase point away from arthritis and towards marrow infiltration, which can present with joint swelling and normal or low white cell counts. Corticosteroids given first partially treat leukaemia, obscure the marrow and worsen risk stratification and outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Leukaemia)

options.text: Arrange ferritin, triglycerides and fibrinogen to assess for macrophage activation syndrome
options.rationale: Macrophage activation syndrome is a genuine cause of cytopenias in a child with arthritis and fever, and this panel is the right way to look for it, but it complicates established systemic arthritis rather than presenting at onset. The severe night bone pain and raised lactate dehydrogenase fit marrow infiltration better. (Source: RCH CPG: Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis)

options.text: Arrange whole body magnetic resonance imaging to map the extent of the bone involvement
options.rationale: Imaging may show marrow signal change but cannot distinguish leukaemic infiltration from chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis or from reactive change, so it does not yield a diagnosis. It also takes longer to organise than the definitive test. (Source: RCH CPG: Leukaemia)

explanation.summary: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia presents with musculoskeletal complaints in a significant minority of children, and a proportion of those are initially labelled as juvenile idiopathic arthritis. The features that should redirect the diagnosis are bone pain that is disproportionate to the joint findings, pain located away from joints, severe night pain that wakes the child, and any cytopenia, particularly when the white cell count is normal or low rather than high. A normal white cell count is not reassuring because blasts may not yet have spilled into the peripheral blood, and the blood film can be unremarkable in early disease. Giving corticosteroids before the marrow is examined is a well-recognised harm: it can induce a partial remission that delays diagnosis, makes the marrow uninterpretable, and is associated with worse outcomes.
key_points: Bone pain away from joints and severe night pain point to marrow disease rather than arthritis
Cytopenia in two or more lines is not a feature of oligoarticular or polyarticular arthritis
A normal white cell count and a bland blood film do not exclude acute leukaemia
Never give corticosteroids for presumed arthritis before excluding leukaemia when red flags are present
Lactate dehydrogenase and uric acid rise with high cell turnover and support the suspicion
explanation.pearls: In children with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia presenting as arthritis, the combination of a platelet count below 150 x10^9/L with a normal or low white cell count and a history of night pain has been shown to discriminate leukaemia from juvenile idiopathic arthritis with high specificity, and any one of those three should stop a steroid prescription.

subtopic_detail: Endometrial thickness threshold triggering tissue sampling in postmenopausal bleeding
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 58-year-old woman who reports two episodes of light vaginal bleeding over the past six weeks, each lasting a day. Her last menstrual period was seven years ago and she has never used menopausal hormone therapy.

Her body mass index is 33 kg/m2 and she has type 2 diabetes managed with metformin. Speculum examination shows a healthy cervix with no visible lesion and a small amount of old blood in the vault, and her cervical screening test from last year was negative for oncogenic human papillomavirus. Transvaginal ultrasound reports a regular endometrial echo measuring 9 mm with no focal lesion and normal ovaries.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 33 kg/m2, healthy cervix with no visible lesion, uterus normal size and mobile, adnexae not palpable
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound shows regular endometrial thickness 9 mm, no focal lesion, both ovaries normal, human papillomavirus screening negative last year

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure her and arrange a repeat transvaginal ultrasound in three months time
options.rationale: A thickness of 9 mm is already well above the threshold at which sampling is indicated, so repeating the same measurement cannot reclassify her. Interval imaging in this setting delays a diagnosis in which stage at presentation drives survival. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding)

options.text: Commence a trial of cyclical oral progestogen and review the bleeding pattern in three months
options.rationale: Progestogen therapy is a treatment for confirmed hyperplasia without atypia and may mask bleeding from an undiagnosed carcinoma. Treating the symptom before establishing the histology removes the only warning sign the patient has. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding)

options.text: Repeat the cervical screening test with reflex cytology and review the result in a month
options.rationale: Cervical screening looks for a different disease at a different site and a negative human papillomavirus result does not address the endometrium at all. Her cervix is visibly healthy, so the bleeding source needs to be sought above the internal os. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)

options.text: Arrange hysteroscopy with endometrial biopsy under the care of a gynaecologist
options.rationale: An endometrial thickness above 4 mm in a woman with postmenopausal bleeding requires tissue diagnosis, and at 9 mm with obesity and diabetes her risk of endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma is substantial. Hysteroscopy allows direct visualisation as well as sampling, which matters because focal lesions can be missed by blind biopsy. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding)

options.text: Request serum CA125 and refer only if the result is above the laboratory reference range
options.rationale: CA125 is used in the assessment of an adnexal mass rather than of endometrial bleeding, and it is neither sensitive nor specific for early endometrial carcinoma. Using a normal result as a gate to referral would falsely reassure. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding)

explanation.summary: Postmenopausal bleeding carries roughly a one in ten risk of endometrial carcinoma and is the symptom that makes this the most curable of the gynaecological cancers, because it declares itself while disease is still confined to the uterus. Transvaginal ultrasound is used as a triage tool rather than a diagnostic one: a thin regular endometrium at or below 4 mm has a high negative predictive value and permits observation, while anything above that threshold requires tissue. Obesity drives risk through peripheral aromatisation of androgens to oestrone in adipose tissue, producing unopposed oestrogen exposure, and diabetes and nulliparity compound it. Recurrent bleeding despite a reassuring initial assessment always warrants repeat investigation, because the negative predictive value applies to a single episode rather than to a pattern.
key_points: Endometrial thickness above 4 mm with postmenopausal bleeding requires tissue sampling
A thickness at or below 4 mm with a single episode of bleeding permits observation
Obesity, diabetes, nulliparity and late menopause all raise endometrial cancer risk
Hysteroscopy adds direct visualisation and detects focal lesions that blind sampling misses
Recurrent bleeding after a reassuring scan mandates repeat assessment regardless
explanation.pearls: Around 90% of women with endometrial carcinoma present with abnormal bleeding, which is why any postmenopausal bleeding warrants investigation within weeks, and why the 4 mm cut-off applies only to women not taking menopausal hormone therapy.

subtopic_detail: Follow-up requirement for an incidental simple ovarian cyst found in a premenopausal woman
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 27-year-old woman who had an abdominal ultrasound last week for intermittent right-sided discomfort that has since settled completely. She has regular 29-day cycles, no intermenstrual bleeding and no change in bowel or bladder habit.

Her abdomen is soft and non-tender with no palpable mass, and a bimanual examination is unremarkable. She has no personal or family history of breast or ovarian cancer. The ultrasound describes a 42 mm unilocular anechoic right ovarian cyst with thin smooth walls, no solid areas, no internal septations and no vascularity on Doppler, with a normal left ovary and no free fluid.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender, no palpable mass, bimanual examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Right ovary contains a 42 mm unilocular anechoic cyst with thin smooth walls, no solid component, no septation, no Doppler flow; left ovary normal; no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to a gynaecologist for consideration of laparoscopic ovarian cystectomy this year
options.rationale: Surgery on a physiological cyst removes normal ovarian cortex and reduces ovarian reserve for no benefit, and carries operative and adhesion risk. Cystectomy is reserved for persistent symptomatic cysts, suspicious features or acute complications. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of Ovarian Cysts)

options.text: Commence a combined oral contraceptive pill to suppress the formation of further cysts
options.rationale: Combined hormonal contraception reduces the incidence of new functional cysts over time but does not hasten resolution of one already present. Prescribing it as treatment for this finding implies the cyst needs treating, which it does not. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of Ovarian Cysts)

options.text: Arrange a repeat transvaginal ultrasound in six weeks to confirm that the cyst has resolved
options.rationale: Repeat imaging is reserved for simple cysts between 50 and 70 mm, which are followed yearly, and for any cyst with complex features. Scanning a 42 mm simple cyst generates incidental findings and anxiety without changing management. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of Ovarian Cysts)

options.text: Request serum CA125 and calculate a risk of malignancy index before deciding on referral
options.rationale: The risk of malignancy index is validated in postmenopausal women and performs poorly before menopause, where CA125 rises with endometriosis, fibroids, menstruation and pelvic inflammation. Applying it to a simple cyst in a young woman generates false positives and unnecessary surgery. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of Ovarian Cysts)

options.text: Reassure her that no further imaging or gynaecology referral is required at this stage
options.rationale: A simple unilocular cyst under 50 mm in a premenopausal woman is a physiological finding that resolves spontaneously in the great majority of cases and carries no malignant potential. Australian and international guidance is explicit that cysts of this size and appearance need no follow-up imaging. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of Ovarian Cysts)

explanation.summary: Ovarian cysts are found incidentally on a large proportion of pelvic scans in women of reproductive age, and most represent the normal physiology of follicular development or corpus luteum formation rather than disease. Sonographic characterisation does most of the diagnostic work: a unilocular anechoic cyst with thin smooth walls, no solid component, no septation and no internal vascularity is described as simple and is effectively never malignant. Size then sets the follow-up, with the commonly used premenopausal thresholds being no follow-up below 50 mm, annual imaging between 50 and 70 mm, and further assessment with magnetic resonance imaging or specialist referral above 70 mm where ultrasound cannot see the whole cyst. The important harm to avoid is overtreatment, since surgery on a young woman's ovary costs follicles permanently.
key_points: Simple premenopausal cysts under 50 mm need no follow-up imaging
Simple cysts of 50 to 70 mm are followed with yearly ultrasound
Cysts above 70 mm warrant magnetic resonance imaging or specialist referral
The risk of malignancy index is validated postmenopausally and misleads before menopause
Any solid component, thick septation or internal vascularity moves the cyst out of the simple category
explanation.pearls: A haemorrhagic corpus luteum cyst shows a characteristic lacy reticular internal pattern with no Doppler flow within the clot, and repeating the scan in the early follicular phase of the next cycle, around day 5 to 10, shows resolution and avoids an unnecessary referral.

sources.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline: Ovarian Cysts in Premenopausal Women

subtopic_detail: Oral iron dosing schedule for a low ferritin identified in the second trimester
stem:
You are the general practitioner providing shared antenatal care for a 29-year-old woman at 20 weeks in her second pregnancy. She feels well, with no bleeding and normal foetal movements, and reports mild tiredness that she attributes to chasing a toddler.

She is vegetarian and her first child was born 14 months ago. Her booking bloods at 11 weeks were normal. Repeat bloods this week show haemoglobin 106 g/L (110-140 in pregnancy), mean cell volume 79 fL (80-100) and ferritin 12 micrograms/L (15-200), with normal C-reactive protein and a normal white cell count and platelet count.

data_table.Examination: Fundal height consistent with dates, foetal heart rate 148/min on Doppler, no pallor of the conjunctivae, no koilonychia
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 106 g/L (110-140), mean cell volume 79 fL (80-100), ferritin 12 micrograms/L (15-200), C-reactive protein 2 mg/L (<5), white cell count and platelet count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Intravenous ferric carboxymaltose given as a single infusion in the day procedure unit
options.rationale: Intravenous iron is indicated when oral iron has failed or is not tolerated, when absorption is impaired, or when the gestation is too advanced for an oral response. At 20 weeks with no oral trial yet, it commits her to an infusion and its risks unnecessarily. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy

options.text: Dietary advice on iron rich foods alone with repeat full blood count at 28 weeks gestation
options.rationale: Diet cannot replete established deficiency within the timeframe of a pregnancy, and non-haem iron from a vegetarian diet is absorbed less efficiently than haem iron. Dietary advice belongs alongside supplementation rather than instead of it. (Source: RANZCOG: Anaemia in Pregnancy)

options.text: Oral elemental iron taken on alternate days on an empty stomach with vitamin C
options.rationale: A ferritin below 30 micrograms/L confirms depleted stores and oral iron is first line in the second trimester when there is time to respond before delivery. Alternate-day dosing produces greater fractional absorption than daily dosing because it avoids the hepcidin rise that a dose triggers for the following 24 hours. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy

options.text: Oral elemental iron taken three times daily with meals to reduce gastrointestinal upset
options.rationale: Divided daily dosing raises hepcidin and reduces the fraction absorbed from each subsequent dose, and taking iron with food further impairs uptake through phytate and calcium binding. The near-pair distinction from the correct approach is dose frequency and timing rather than the drug itself. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy

options.text: Serum folate and vitamin B12 assay with treatment deferred until those results return
options.rationale: Folate and B12 deficiency cause macrocytosis rather than the microcytosis present here, and B12 is worth checking in a vegetarian but does not explain these indices. Deferring iron for a fortnight while a parallel test returns wastes treatment time. (Source: RANZCOG: Anaemia in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Iron requirements roughly triple across pregnancy to supply expanded maternal red cell mass, the foetus and the placenta, and a short interpregnancy interval means stores have had little chance to recover. Ferritin is the best single measure of iron stores but is an acute phase reactant, so a normal or raised value alongside a normal C-reactive protein is interpretable while a raised value with inflammation is not. Treatment matters beyond maternal symptoms, because antenatal iron deficiency is associated with low birth weight, preterm birth and reduced neonatal iron endowment that affects infant development. The hepcidin response to an oral dose suppresses absorption for around 24 hours, which is the physiological basis for alternate-day rather than divided daily dosing.
key_points: Ferritin below 30 micrograms/L indicates deficiency even when haemoglobin is only mildly reduced
Oral iron on alternate days is absorbed more efficiently than the same total dose split daily
Take iron away from food, tea, coffee and calcium, with vitamin C to aid absorption
Intravenous iron is for oral failure, intolerance, malabsorption or late gestation
Ferritin is an acute phase reactant, so interpret it alongside C-reactive protein
explanation.pearls: Expect a haemoglobin rise of about 10 g/L within 2 to 4 weeks of starting adequate oral iron, and treat failure to achieve that as a trigger to check adherence and reconsider the diagnosis rather than simply escalating the dose.

sources.label: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy

subtopic_detail: First line therapy for heavy menstrual bleeding when the uterine cavity is structurally normal
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34-year-old woman who describes flooding through a super tampon and a pad every hour on her two heaviest days, with clots the size of a twenty cent coin and two days off work each cycle. Her cycles are regular at 28 days.

She has completed her family and would prefer not to become pregnant, though she is not seeking permanent contraception. Pelvic examination is normal with a normal sized mobile uterus. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a normal uterus with an endometrium of 6 mm, no fibroid and no polyp. Her haemoglobin is 108 g/L (115-155) with ferritin 9 micrograms/L (15-200), and thyroid function and coagulation screen are within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Normal sized mobile uterus, no adnexal mass, cervix healthy
