data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound shows normal uterus, endometrium 6 mm, no fibroid or polyp; haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-155); ferritin 9 micrograms/L (15-200); thyroid function and coagulation screen within normal limits

lead_in: Which treatment would you recommend first?

options.text: Oral non-steroidal anti-inflammatory therapy started on the first day of each period
options.rationale: Non-steroidal agents reduce blood loss by around a fifth and help dysmenorrhoea, making them useful adjuncts, but they are the weakest of the medical options for volume. Used alone they are unlikely to correct bleeding severe enough to cause this degree of iron depletion. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

options.text: Oral norethisterone taken from day five to day twenty six of each menstrual cycle
options.rationale: Long-course oral progestogen does reduce bleeding but requires daily tablets for three weeks of every cycle, is poorly tolerated and is less effective than an intrauterine device. Short luteal-phase courses are ineffective and should not be used at all. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

options.text: Referral for endometrial ablation after counselling about future pregnancy implications
options.rationale: Ablation is effective but is a surgical procedure that mandates reliable contraception afterwards because pregnancy following ablation carries serious risk. It is considered after medical therapy has failed rather than before it has been tried. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

options.text: Insertion of a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system at her next convenient visit
options.rationale: The levonorgestrel intrauterine system reduces menstrual blood loss more than any other medical therapy and is first line for heavy bleeding with a structurally normal cavity. It simultaneously provides the contraception she wants without committing her to a permanent procedure. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

options.text: Oral tranexamic acid taken during the heaviest days of each menstrual period only
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid reduces blood loss by roughly a third and is a reasonable option for a woman wanting non-hormonal treatment or trying to conceive, but the magnitude of benefit is smaller and it provides no contraception. It is the alternative when an intrauterine device is declined or unsuitable. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

explanation.summary: Heavy menstrual bleeding is defined by its impact on a woman's physical, social and emotional quality of life rather than by a measured volume, so the history of flooding, clots and time off work is the diagnosis. The PALM-COEIN system separates structural causes, which are polyps, adenomyosis, leiomyoma and malignancy, from non-structural ones including coagulopathy, ovulatory dysfunction, endometrial and iatrogenic causes, and it directs the workup. A normal ultrasound with regular ovulatory cycles points to a primary endometrial disorder of haemostasis, which is the setting in which the levonorgestrel intrauterine system performs best. Iron deficiency is present in a large proportion of these women and must be treated alongside the bleeding rather than assumed to resolve with it.
key_points: Heavy menstrual bleeding is defined by quality of life impact, not by measured millilitres
The levonorgestrel intrauterine system is first line when the cavity is structurally normal
Tranexamic acid and non-steroidal agents are non-hormonal options for women avoiding hormones or seeking pregnancy
Short luteal-phase progestogen courses are ineffective for heavy bleeding
Treat coexisting iron deficiency in parallel rather than waiting for bleeding to settle
explanation.pearls: Around one in five women presenting with heavy menstrual bleeding since menarche has an underlying bleeding disorder, most commonly von Willebrand disease, so bleeding that dates from the very first period warrants a coagulation screen and von Willebrand studies rather than empirical treatment alone.

subtopic_detail: Colposcopy pathway after human papillomavirus types 16 or 18 on a self collected screening sample
stem:
You are the general practitioner contacting a 41-year-old woman with her cervical screening result. She chose self collection because she had found previous speculum examinations distressing, and this was her first screening test in eleven years.

She has no abnormal bleeding, no discharge and no pain, and she is not pregnant. Her only previous screening results were normal cytology on two occasions in her twenties. The laboratory reports oncogenic human papillomavirus detected, type 16, with a note that reflex cytology could not be performed on the self collected specimen.

data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening test on a self collected vaginal sample: oncogenic human papillomavirus detected, type 16; reflex liquid based cytology not performed on this specimen type

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the human papillomavirus test in twelve months to see whether the infection clears
options.rationale: Twelve month repeat testing applies to women with oncogenic types other than 16 and 18 whose reflex cytology is negative or low grade. Applying it to a type 16 result in a woman screened once in eleven years risks allowing established high grade disease to progress. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)

options.text: Refer directly for colposcopy without arranging any further sampling beforehand
options.rationale: Detection of human papillomavirus type 16 or 18 leads straight to colposcopy regardless of cytology, because these two types account for the large majority of cervical cancers and confer the highest immediate risk of high grade disease. The absence of reflex cytology on a self collected sample does not alter that pathway. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)

options.text: Offer human papillomavirus vaccination now and repeat screening in twelve months time
options.rationale: Vaccination is prophylactic and does not clear an infection that is already established or treat existing cervical disease. Offering it as an alternative to assessment misapplies a preventive intervention to a diagnostic problem. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)

options.text: Repeat the self collected sample now to confirm the result before making any referral
options.rationale: Self collected samples tested with a polymerase chain reaction assay have equivalent sensitivity for high grade disease to clinician collected samples, so the result does not need confirmation. Repeating it duplicates a reliable test and postpones definitive assessment. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)

options.text: Arrange a clinician collected sample for liquid based cytology and refer if it is abnormal
options.rationale: Cytology triage determines management for the other oncogenic types, where a negative or low grade result allows a 12-month repeat, but types 16 and 18 bypass that triage entirely. Waiting on cytology here would delay colposcopy without any possibility of changing the destination. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)

explanation.summary: The Australian National Cervical Screening Program uses primary human papillomavirus testing every five years from age 25 to 74, with partial genotyping that separates types 16 and 18 from the other oncogenic types. That split exists because 16 and 18 cause around 70% of cervical cancers and carry a much higher risk of prevalent high grade disease, so they are referred to colposcopy immediately while the other types are triaged on cytology. Self collection is now available to every screening participant as a way of reaching women who have been under-screened, and its performance for high grade disease is equivalent to clinician collection. Reflex cytology cannot be performed on a self collected vaginal sample, so a woman needing cytology triage must return for a clinician collected specimen, but that requirement does not apply when the result is type 16 or 18.
key_points: Human papillomavirus 16 or 18 detected means direct colposcopy referral irrespective of cytology
Other oncogenic types are triaged with reflex cytology and often repeated at 12 months
Self collection has equivalent sensitivity for high grade disease and is available to all participants
Reflex cytology is not possible on a self collected sample, so cytology triage needs a clinician collected one
Under-screened women carry the highest burden of cervical cancer in Australia
explanation.pearls: Cervical screening starts at 25 years or two years after first sexual activity if later, and in Australia any symptomatic woman with abnormal bleeding or postcoital bleeding needs a co-test with cytology and speculum examination regardless of when she last screened.

subtopic_detail: Where to operate on a complex adnexal mass with a high risk of malignancy index after menopause
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar assessing a 64-year-old woman referred with four months of abdominal bloating, early satiety and a 5 kg unintentional weight loss. She went through menopause at 51 and has never used hormone therapy.

Her abdomen is distended with shifting dullness and a firm irregular mass palpable in the right iliac fossa. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a 92 mm multilocular right adnexal mass with solid papillary projections and marked internal vascularity, together with moderate ascites. Serum CA125 is 640 kU/L (<35). A computed tomography scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis shows omental thickening but no parenchymal liver or lung lesion.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88/min, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Distended abdomen with shifting dullness, firm irregular right iliac fossa mass, no palpable supraclavicular nodes
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound: 92 mm multilocular right adnexal mass with solid papillary projections and marked vascularity, moderate ascites; CA125 640 kU/L (<35); computed tomography shows omental thickening without liver or lung metastases

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Request magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis to further characterise the adnexal mass
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is valuable when ultrasound findings are indeterminate and the mass could be a fibroid, an endometrioma or a dermoid, which is not the case here. Adding a fourth imaging study to an already convincing picture only delays referral. (Source: RANZCOG: Assessment of Adnexal Masses)

options.text: Arrange therapeutic paracentesis with cytology and review her again once the result returns
options.rationale: Ascitic cytology can be useful when neoadjuvant chemotherapy is being considered and a tissue diagnosis is needed without surgery, but that decision belongs to the oncology team. A negative cytology does not exclude malignancy, so a normal result would not change the referral. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian Cancer Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian Cancer Guidelines

options.text: Refer to a gynaecological oncology centre for multidisciplinary assessment and surgery
options.rationale: Her risk of malignancy index is far above the threshold of 200 that mandates specialist referral, combining a postmenopausal score, a CA125 of 640 kU/L and multiple suspicious ultrasound features. Survival is measurably better when cytoreductive surgery for ovarian cancer is performed by a subspecialist in a centre with the full multidisciplinary team. (Source: RANZCOG: Assessment of Adnexal Masses)

options.text: Repeat the CA125 in six weeks and refer if the value has risen above the current level
options.rationale: Serial CA125 has a role in monitoring treatment response and detecting recurrence, not in deciding whether to investigate a suspicious mass. A six week delay in a woman with ascites and omental disease allows measurable progression. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian Cancer Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian Cancer Guidelines

options.text: Arrange laparoscopic oophorectomy on the local gynaecology list within the next two weeks
options.rationale: Operating locally on a likely advanced ovarian malignancy risks incomplete staging, tumour rupture with upstaging, and port site seeding, and a general list cannot deliver the debulking these women need. Speed is valuable but does not compensate for the wrong operation in the wrong place. (Source: RANZCOG: Assessment of Adnexal Masses)

explanation.summary: Ovarian cancer is the gynaecological malignancy with the poorest survival in Australia, largely because the early symptoms of bloating, early satiety, urinary urgency and abdominal pain are non-specific and commonly attributed to gastrointestinal causes for months. The risk of malignancy index multiplies a menopausal score, an ultrasound morphology score and the CA125 value, and a result above 200 is the accepted trigger for referral to a gynaecological oncology service. The reason the destination matters so much is that survival correlates strongly with the completeness of cytoreduction, which requires a surgeon able to perform bowel resection, splenectomy and diaphragmatic stripping as needed. Where disease is too extensive for primary debulking, neoadjuvant chemotherapy with interval surgery is the alternative, and that decision is made by the multidisciplinary team rather than at the point of referral.
key_points: A risk of malignancy index above 200 mandates gynaecological oncology referral
The index combines menopausal status, ultrasound morphology score and CA125
Survival improves when surgery is performed by a subspecialist in a specialist centre
Bloating, early satiety and abdominal pain lasting weeks warrant investigation in women over 50
Completeness of cytoreduction is the strongest surgical determinant of outcome
explanation.pearls: Any woman diagnosed with high grade serous ovarian cancer in Australia should be offered germline and tumour BRCA1 and BRCA2 testing at diagnosis, because a pathogenic variant both opens access to PARP inhibitor maintenance therapy and triggers cascade testing of her relatives.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian Cancer Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Reading a raised CA125 against a suspected endometrioma before menopause
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 31-year-old woman referred by her general practitioner with a raised tumour marker and a request for urgent oncology assessment. She has had severe period pain since her teens, deep pain with intercourse and pain on opening her bowels during menstruation.

She has been trying to conceive for 18 months. Her appetite and weight are stable and there is no bloating or early satiety. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a 46 mm right ovarian cyst with homogeneous low level internal echoes, no solid papillary projection and no internal vascularity, with the ovary tethered to the uterus on probe pressure. Serum CA125 is 118 kU/L (<35).

data_table.Examination: Tender nodularity palpable in the posterior fornix, fixed retroverted uterus, right adnexal tenderness, no ascites, no abdominal mass
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound: 46 mm right ovarian cyst with homogeneous low level internal echoes, no solid component, no internal vascularity, reduced ovarian mobility; CA125 118 kU/L (<35); full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate interpretation and next step?

options.text: The finding requires tissue; arrange ultrasound guided cyst aspiration with fluid cytology
options.rationale: Aspiration of an endometrioma yields old altered blood that is unhelpful cytologically, and recurrence after aspiration alone approaches certainty. Puncturing a cyst that has not been excluded as malignant also risks peritoneal spill. (Source: RANZCOG: Assessment of Adnexal Masses)

options.text: The marker is raised by benign disease; plan fertility focused gynaecology management
options.rationale: CA125 is expressed by any inflamed coelomic epithelium, so endometriosis, fibroids, pelvic infection, menstruation and pregnancy all raise it, and the risk of malignancy index is not validated before menopause. The ground glass appearance without vascularity and the fixed tender pelvis describe an endometrioma in a woman whose pressing clinical problem is subfertility. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis Clinical Guideline)

options.text: The marker is non-diagnostic; arrange serial measurement every six weeks for six months
options.rationale: CA125 fluctuates with the menstrual cycle and with disease activity in endometriosis, so serial values in this setting generate noise rather than information. There is no threshold or trajectory that would reclassify a sonographically benign endometrioma. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis Clinical Guideline)

options.text: The marker indicates likely malignancy; refer urgently to a gynaecological oncology centre
options.rationale: Subspecialist referral is driven by a high risk of malignancy index in a postmenopausal woman or by suspicious morphology such as solid papillary projections, thick septations, vascularity or ascites, none of which is present. Referring on the marker alone would subject a young woman to oncological surgery for benign disease. (Source: RANZCOG: Assessment of Adnexal Masses)

options.text: The finding needs suppression; start a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist for six months
options.rationale: Medical suppression reduces endometriosis-associated pain but induces a hypo-oestrogenic state that prevents conception, which directly opposes her goal of pregnancy. It also shrinks endometriomas only modestly and they recur on cessation. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis Clinical Guideline)

explanation.summary: CA125 is a glycoprotein shed by mesothelial and Mullerian epithelium under almost any inflammatory stimulus, so its specificity for ovarian cancer is poor in premenopausal women and good only after menopause, when the benign causes largely disappear. That difference is why the risk of malignancy index is validated postmenopausally and why applying it to a young woman with endometriosis produces a false alarm. The sonographic appearance carries far more weight than the marker: an endometrioma shows homogeneous low level ground glass echoes with no solid component and no internal Doppler flow, and site-specific tenderness and reduced ovarian mobility on the probe add to the picture. Managing this woman well means addressing pain and subfertility together, since surgical excision of an endometrioma removes healthy cortex and can lower ovarian reserve, so the decision to operate is weighed against assisted reproduction.
key_points: CA125 rises in endometriosis, fibroids, pelvic inflammatory disease, menstruation and pregnancy
The risk of malignancy index is validated after menopause and misleads before it
Ground glass internal echoes with no solid component or vascularity characterise an endometrioma
Site-specific tenderness and reduced ovarian mobility indicate adhesive pelvic disease
Endometrioma excision can reduce ovarian reserve, so weigh surgery against assisted reproduction
explanation.pearls: Ovarian endometriomas larger than 3 cm reduce antral follicle count in the affected ovary even before surgery, so an anti-Mullerian hormone level measured before any planned cystectomy gives the couple a realistic baseline for counselling about fertility outcomes.

subtopic_detail: Tumour based mismatch repair testing after endometrial carcinoma diagnosed before age fifty
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 46-year-old woman two weeks after a total hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy for endometrioid endometrial carcinoma, reported as grade 1 with less than half myometrial invasion and no lymphovascular space invasion.

She is recovering well with no complications. Her body mass index is 24 kg/m2, she has had three pregnancies and she has never had diabetes or polycystic ovary syndrome. Her father had bowel cancer at 52 and a paternal aunt had a uterine cancer in her forties. She asks whether her two daughters need to do anything.

data_table.Examination: Abdominal wounds healing well, no collection, no pelvic tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Histology: grade 1 endometrioid adenocarcinoma, myometrial invasion less than 50%, no lymphovascular space invasion, margins clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure her that the family history is on the paternal side and carries no risk to daughters
options.rationale: Lynch syndrome is autosomal dominant and transmitted equally through the paternal line, so a father with early bowel cancer is as informative as a mother would be. This is a common misconception about gynaecological cancer risk that leads to missed diagnoses. (Source: eviQ: Lynch Syndrome Risk Management)

options.text: Request mismatch repair immunohistochemistry on the hysterectomy tumour specimen
options.rationale: Endometrial cancer is the sentinel malignancy in around half of women with Lynch syndrome, and her age under 50 with a father and aunt affected by Lynch spectrum cancers raises that possibility strongly. Immunohistochemistry for the four mismatch repair proteins on existing tumour tissue is the standard first triage test and requires no new sample. (Source: eviQ: Lynch Syndrome Risk Management)

options.text: Request germline gene panel testing on a blood sample from her before any tumour testing
options.rationale: Germline testing is the confirmatory step and is appropriate once tumour triage suggests mismatch repair deficiency or when family history alone is compelling enough to bypass triage. Going straight to a blood panel in every case tests many women whose tumours are mismatch repair proficient. (Source: eviQ: Lynch Syndrome Risk Management)

options.text: Arrange adjuvant vaginal vault brachytherapy and defer any genetic discussion until after it
options.rationale: Grade 1 disease with superficial invasion and no lymphovascular space invasion is low risk and does not usually require adjuvant radiotherapy at all. The genetic question is independent of adjuvant treatment and should not be deferred behind it. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial Cancer Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial Cancer Guidelines

options.text: Arrange colonoscopy for her and for both daughters within the next twelve month period
options.rationale: Colonoscopic surveillance is exactly what a confirmed diagnosis would trigger, but the interval and starting age depend on which gene is involved, and testing unaffected daughters before the family variant is known is uninformative. The sequence runs from tumour to germline to cascade testing. (Source: eviQ: Lynch Syndrome Risk Management)

explanation.summary: Lynch syndrome results from a germline pathogenic variant in one of the mismatch repair genes MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 or PMS2, or in EPCAM, and it substantially raises lifetime risk of colorectal, endometrial, ovarian, gastric, urothelial and other cancers. Endometrial cancer precedes the colorectal cancer in a large share of affected women, which makes the gynaecologist the person most likely to make the diagnosis for the whole family. Testing follows a sequence: immunohistochemistry or microsatellite instability testing on tumour tissue, then MLH1 promoter methylation analysis when MLH1 and PMS2 are both lost to distinguish sporadic epigenetic silencing from inherited disease, and finally germline testing. Identifying a variant changes management for the patient through colonoscopic surveillance and aspirin chemoprophylaxis, and for relatives through cascade testing and risk-reducing surgery.
key_points: Endometrial cancer is the sentinel cancer in about half of women with Lynch syndrome
Tumour mismatch repair immunohistochemistry is the first triage test and uses existing tissue
Loss of MLH1 and PMS2 needs promoter methylation testing to separate sporadic from inherited causes
Lynch syndrome is autosomal dominant and transmitted through either parent
Confirmation triggers colonoscopic surveillance, aspirin prophylaxis and cascade family testing
explanation.pearls: Regular aspirin reduces colorectal cancer incidence in Lynch syndrome by around half with the benefit emerging after several years of use, which is why it is offered to confirmed carriers alongside one to two yearly colonoscopy starting at 25 years for MLH1 and MSH2 carriers.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial Cancer Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Switching from oral to intravenous iron in the third trimester after gastrointestinal intolerance
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the antenatal clinic reviewing a 33-year-old woman at 30 weeks in her fourth pregnancy. She was started on oral iron at 22 weeks but stopped after ten days because of severe constipation and epigastric pain, and a second preparation caused the same problem.

She reports increasing breathlessness climbing stairs and has a placenta that was reported as low lying at her morphology scan, with a repeat scan booked for 34 weeks. Her bloods today show haemoglobin 86 g/L (110-140 in pregnancy), mean cell volume 74 fL (80-100) and ferritin 6 micrograms/L (15-200), with normal C-reactive protein, normal B12 and folate, and a normal haemoglobin electrophoresis performed at booking.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104/min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 C, foetal heart rate 145/min
data_table.Examination: Fundal height consistent with dates, cephalic presentation, pale conjunctivae, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 86 g/L (110-140), mean cell volume 74 fL (80-100), ferritin 6 micrograms/L (15-200), C-reactive protein 3 mg/L (<5), B12 and folate within normal limits, haemoglobin electrophoresis normal at booking

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment now?

options.text: Recombinant human erythropoietin given subcutaneously with oral iron supplementation
options.rationale: Erythropoiesis stimulating agents are used in anaemia of chronic kidney disease rather than in uncomplicated iron deficiency, where the limiting factor is substrate rather than erythropoietin. Giving it alongside oral iron she cannot absorb compounds the error. (Source: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines)
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines

options.text: A third oral iron preparation taken with food to improve gastrointestinal tolerability
options.rationale: Two preparations have already failed for the same reason, and taking iron with food to reduce symptoms substantially reduces the fraction absorbed. Persisting orally spends weeks she does not have before delivery. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy

options.text: Transfusion of two units of packed red cells arranged as an elective admission this week
options.rationale: Transfusion is reserved for symptomatic severe anaemia near delivery, active bleeding or haemodynamic compromise, and it carries alloimmunisation risk that matters in a woman who may have further pregnancies. She is stable, so iron replacement is the correct pathway. (Source: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines)
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines

options.text: Repeat the full blood count and ferritin in four weeks before committing to any treatment
options.rationale: The diagnosis is already secure with a microcytic anaemia, a ferritin of 6 micrograms/L and a normal C-reactive protein, so repeat testing adds nothing. Four weeks of observation takes her to 34 weeks with untreated severe anaemia and a possible placenta praevia. (Source: RANZCOG: Anaemia in Pregnancy)

options.text: Intravenous iron infusion arranged in the day unit within the coming week
options.rationale: She has documented intolerance of two oral preparations, a haemoglobin of 86 g/L and only ten weeks left, which is too little time for oral therapy to correct stores even if she could take it. Intravenous iron is safe from the second trimester onwards and raises haemoglobin faster and more completely than oral replacement. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy

explanation.summary: Antenatal iron deficiency anaemia matters most for what it does to a woman's tolerance of blood loss at delivery, since postpartum haemorrhage is common and a woman entering labour with a haemoglobin of 86 g/L has no reserve. Intravenous iron preparations such as ferric carboxymaltose deliver a large replacement dose in a single short infusion and are established as safe after the first trimester, with the main issues being transient hypophosphataemia, infusion reactions and skin staining from extravasation. The threshold for moving from oral to intravenous therapy is set by intolerance, malabsorption, failure to respond, severity of the anaemia, and how much time remains before delivery. A low lying placenta adds weight to correcting the anaemia early, because it raises the probability of significant peripartum bleeding.
key_points: Intravenous iron is indicated for oral intolerance, malabsorption, non-response or late gestation
It is considered safe from the second trimester onwards
Transfusion is reserved for haemodynamic compromise, active bleeding or severe symptomatic anaemia near delivery
Antenatal anaemia reduces tolerance of postpartum haemorrhage and increases transfusion need
Confirm the diagnosis with ferritin plus C-reactive protein before infusing
explanation.pearls: Ferric carboxymaltose causes transient hypophosphataemia in a substantial minority of recipients, so a woman needing repeat infusions or reporting persistent bone pain or weakness afterwards should have a serum phosphate checked rather than being given more iron.

sources.label: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Iron Deficiency in Pregnancy
National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Operative approach to a submucosal fibroid distorting the cavity in a woman wanting pregnancy
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 36-year-old woman with two years of progressively heavier periods and two early miscarriages. She has been trying to conceive for a third pregnancy for the past year.

She has already completed a six month trial of tranexamic acid with only partial benefit and declines hormonal treatment because she wants to conceive. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a 26 mm fibroid that appeared to indent the cavity, and a subsequent saline infusion sonohysterogram confirms a submucosal fibroid with more than half of its volume within the cavity and a normal outer myometrial margin. Her haemoglobin is 104 g/L (115-155).

data_table.Examination: Bulky uterus approximately 8 week size, mobile and non-tender, no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Saline infusion sonohysterogram: 26 mm submucosal fibroid with more than 50% intracavitary component, remainder of cavity normal; haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-155); ferritin 11 micrograms/L (15-200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate definitive management?

options.text: Hysteroscopic resection of the fibroid performed transcervically under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: A submucosal fibroid with more than half of its volume in the cavity is accessible transcervically, and hysteroscopic resection removes it without any uterine incision, preserving the myometrium for a future pregnancy. Submucosal fibroids are the subtype with the clearest adverse effect on both bleeding and implantation, so removal addresses her two problems together. (Source: RANZCOG: Uterine Fibroids)

options.text: Gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist therapy for six months to shrink the fibroid
options.rationale: Agonist therapy shrinks fibroids and corrects anaemia before surgery, which is a legitimate adjunct, but the effect reverses on cessation and the drug prevents conception while it is given. It is preparation for an operation rather than a definitive treatment. (Source: RANZCOG: Uterine Fibroids)

options.text: Laparoscopic myomectomy with layered closure of the resulting myometrial defect
options.rationale: Abdominal or laparoscopic myomectomy is the approach for intramural and subserosal fibroids that cannot be reached from the cavity, and it creates a myometrial scar that raises the small risk of uterine rupture in labour. Choosing it for a predominantly intracavitary fibroid imposes an unnecessary uterine incision. (Source: RANZCOG: Uterine Fibroids)

options.text: Endometrial ablation with a second generation device following endometrial preparation
options.rationale: Ablation destroys the endometrium and is absolutely contraindicated in a woman planning pregnancy, since subsequent conception carries high rates of abnormal placentation and loss. It also performs poorly when the cavity is distorted by a submucosal fibroid. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

options.text: Uterine artery embolisation performed by interventional radiology as a day case procedure
options.rationale: Embolisation is effective for bleeding and bulk symptoms but is relatively contraindicated when future fertility is desired, because of effects on ovarian reserve and on placentation. A submucosal fibroid can also slough after embolisation and cause prolonged discharge or infection. (Source: RANZCOG: Uterine Fibroids)

explanation.summary: Fibroid management is driven by location far more than by size, which is why the submucosal, intramural and subserosal distinction and the degree of intracavitary extension determine the operation. Submucosal fibroids distort the cavity and disrupt the endometrium, producing heavy bleeding and interfering with implantation, and they are the group for which removal has the clearest fertility benefit. Saline infusion sonohysterography or hysteroscopy is needed to grade the intracavitary component because standard ultrasound often cannot tell an intramural fibroid indenting the cavity from a true submucosal one. Where more than half the fibroid lies within the cavity the lesion can usually be resected in a single hysteroscopic procedure, whereas a deeper lesion may need a staged approach to avoid perforation and excessive fluid absorption.
key_points: Location rather than size determines the operative approach to fibroids
Submucosal fibroids cause heavy bleeding and impair implantation
Saline infusion sonohysterography grades the intracavitary component before surgery
Hysteroscopic resection avoids a myometrial incision and preserves the uterus for pregnancy
Embolisation and ablation are both unsuitable when future fertility is desired
explanation.pearls: Fluid deficit is monitored continuously during hysteroscopic resection because absorption of hypotonic distension medium causes dilutional hyponatraemia and cerebral oedema, and the procedure is stopped at a deficit of around 1000 mL with hypotonic fluid in a healthy woman.

subtopic_detail: Adnexal torsion where preserved Doppler arterial flow argues against the diagnosis
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar called to the emergency department to see a 24-year-old woman with eight hours of severe right iliac fossa pain that began abruptly while she was at the gym, with three episodes of vomiting. The pain has waxed and waned in intensity but has never fully settled.

Her last menstrual period was three weeks ago and a urinary pregnancy test is negative. She had a 6 cm right ovarian dermoid documented on a scan two years ago that she elected to leave alone. On examination she is tender in the right iliac fossa with guarding. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an enlarged oedematous right ovary measuring 78 mm containing the known dermoid, with a small volume of free fluid, and the report notes that arterial and venous Doppler flow are both demonstrable within the ovary.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 106/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.2 C
data_table.Examination: Right iliac fossa tenderness with voluntary guarding, no rebound, cervix closed with no bleeding, right adnexal tenderness on bimanual examination
data_table.Investigations: Urinary pregnancy test negative, white cell count 13.1 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 14 mg/L (<5), transvaginal ultrasound shows 78 mm oedematous right ovary containing a dermoid, free fluid present, arterial and venous Doppler flow both demonstrable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit for observation with analgesia and repeat the Doppler ultrasound in twelve hours
options.rationale: Waiting for arterial flow to disappear means waiting for the ovary to infarct, since loss of arterial signal is a late finding rather than the diagnostic threshold. The waxing and waning pain characteristic of intermittent torsion is precisely the window in which surgery preserves the ovary. (Source: RANZCOG: Acute Pelvic Pain)

options.text: Request computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis to exclude appendicitis first
options.rationale: Appendicitis is a reasonable differential given the right sided pain and mild inflammatory response, but the ultrasound has already identified an enlarged oedematous ovary containing a known mass, which explains the presentation. Imaging that irradiates a young woman while the ovary twists trades a small diagnostic gain for a large time cost. (Source: RANZCOG: Acute Pelvic Pain)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis to confirm the diagnosis before operating
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging can show ovarian oedema and a twisted pedicle, but obtaining it out of hours is slow and it changes nothing about the need for surgery in a patient with this history and these findings. No imaging result would make observation safe. (Source: RANZCOG: Acute Pelvic Pain)

options.text: Proceed to diagnostic laparoscopy with a view to untwisting and conserving the ovary
options.rationale: Preserved Doppler flow does not exclude torsion, because the ovary has a dual blood supply from the ovarian and uterine arteries and venous and lymphatic obstruction precede arterial compromise, producing the oedematous enlargement seen here. Torsion is a clinical and surgical diagnosis, and untwisting rather than removing the ovary is now standard because the great majority regain function even when the ovary looks dusky. (Source: RANZCOG: Acute Pelvic Pain)

options.text: Commence intravenous antibiotics for presumed pelvic inflammatory disease and review tomorrow
options.rationale: Pelvic inflammatory disease typically produces bilateral pain with cervical motion tenderness, discharge and a more indolent onset rather than abrupt pain during exertion with vomiting. The mildly raised white cell count here reflects the stress response and tissue ischaemia rather than infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Ovarian torsion is the gynaecological emergency most often missed, and the single commonest reason is misplaced confidence in Doppler ultrasound. The ovary receives blood from both the ovarian artery and the ovarian branch of the uterine artery, so arterial flow is frequently still detectable in a torted ovary, and because the thin walled veins and lymphatics obstruct before the arteries do, the earliest and most reliable sonographic sign is unilateral ovarian enlargement with stromal oedema rather than absent flow. Most torsion occurs around a lead point, typically a benign cyst or dermoid between 5 and 10 cm, since very large masses are less mobile and small ovaries rarely twist. Management has shifted decisively towards conservative detorsion even when the ovary appears necrotic, because gross appearance correlates poorly with recoverable function and the risk of thromboembolism from untwisting has not been borne out.
key_points: Present Doppler flow does not exclude torsion because of the dual arterial supply
Unilateral ovarian enlargement with stromal oedema is the more reliable sonographic sign
Waxing and waning severe pain suggests intermittent torsion and should not reassure
A lead point mass of 5 to 10 cm is the usual precipitant
Detorsion with ovarian conservation is preferred over oophorectomy even for a dusky ovary
explanation.pearls: Oophoropexy is considered after detorsion when there is no lead point mass, when torsion is recurrent, or when the contralateral ovary has already been lost, since the underlying problem in those cases is an abnormally long utero-ovarian ligament rather than the mass itself.

subtopic_detail: Assessing bleeding on tamoxifen where the usual endometrial thickness cut-off is not applicable
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 62-year-old woman with a single episode of vaginal spotting last week. She completed treatment for an oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer three years ago and takes tamoxifen 20 mg daily, which she is due to continue for a further two years.

She went through menopause at 50 and has no other bleeding, no discharge and no pain. Speculum examination shows a healthy cervix with no visible lesion. Transvaginal ultrasound reports an endometrial thickness of 11 mm with a cystic heterogeneous appearance and poorly defined margins, and the sonographer comments that the endometrial-myometrial interface is difficult to resolve. The ovaries are normal and there is no free fluid.

data_table.Examination: Healthy cervix with no visible lesion, uterus normal size and mobile, adnexae not palpable, no inguinal lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound: endometrial thickness 11 mm, cystic heterogeneous appearance, indistinct endometrial-myometrial interface, ovaries normal, no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Contact her oncologist to switch tamoxifen to an aromatase inhibitor and rescan afterwards
options.rationale: Switching to an aromatase inhibitor removes the endometrial stimulus and may well be discussed once the histology is known, but changing adjuvant breast cancer therapy does not investigate the bleeding that has already occurred. The sequence is to obtain tissue first and involve the oncologist afterwards. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial Cancer Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial Cancer Guidelines

options.text: Arrange hysteroscopy with directed biopsy irrespective of the measured endometrial thickness
options.rationale: Tamoxifen produces subendometrial stromal cystic change that inflates the sonographic measurement and blurs the interface, so the thickness threshold used in other postmenopausal women is not valid and cannot be used to triage her. Hysteroscopy allows the cavity to be seen directly and focal lesions to be sampled under vision, which blind sampling would miss. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding)

options.text: Request magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis to assess for myometrial invasion first
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging stages a carcinoma that has already been diagnosed histologically and cannot distinguish benign tamoxifen change from malignancy. Using it as a diagnostic filter ahead of tissue reverses the order of assessment. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial Cancer Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial Cancer Guidelines

options.text: Reassure her that the appearance is a recognised drug effect and repeat the scan in six months
options.rationale: The sonographic appearance is indeed a recognised tamoxifen effect, but she has bled, and bleeding is the symptom that demands tissue regardless of how well the imaging is explained. Attributing a symptom to a known drug effect without excluding malignancy is the central error in this scenario. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding)

options.text: Arrange outpatient pipelle endometrial sampling and manage according to the histology
options.rationale: Blind pipelle sampling detects diffuse disease well but samples only a fraction of the cavity, and the lesions tamoxifen causes are characteristically focal polyps rather than a uniform process. A benign pipelle result would therefore not exclude a focal carcinoma. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of Postmenopausal Bleeding)

explanation.summary: Tamoxifen acts as a selective oestrogen receptor modulator, antagonising the receptor in breast tissue while behaving as a partial agonist in the endometrium, which is why it both reduces breast cancer recurrence and raises endometrial cancer risk several-fold in postmenopausal women. It characteristically produces subendometrial stromal hypertrophy with cystic change, endometrial polyps and adenomyotic change, all of which thicken and distort the sonographic endometrial stripe without any malignancy being present. The practical consequence is that the 4 mm triage threshold, which depends on a thin uniform endometrium having a high negative predictive value, breaks down entirely in these women, and ultrasound cannot be used to decide who needs sampling. Asymptomatic women on tamoxifen are not screened with ultrasound for the same reason, since it generates procedures without improving outcomes, but any bleeding is investigated promptly.
key_points: Tamoxifen is an endometrial partial agonist and raises endometrial cancer risk after menopause
It causes subendometrial cystic change that invalidates the usual thickness threshold
Any bleeding on tamoxifen requires hysteroscopy and directed biopsy, not ultrasound triage
Lesions are often focal polyps, so blind sampling can miss them
Asymptomatic women on tamoxifen are not screened with ultrasound
explanation.pearls: Aromatase inhibitors such as anastrozole do not carry the endometrial risk of tamoxifen because they lower oestrogen synthesis rather than acting at the receptor, which is one reason a postmenopausal woman who develops endometrial pathology on tamoxifen is often switched rather than simply monitored.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Endometrial Cancer Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Booking microcytosis with replete iron stores requiring haemoglobinopathy evaluation of the couple
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing booking bloods for a 26-year-old woman at 9 weeks in her first pregnancy. She feels well apart from mild nausea and has no bleeding.

She was born in Australia and her parents came from southern Italy. She was told as a teenager that she was anaemic and took iron tablets for a year without any change in her blood count. Today her haemoglobin is 103 g/L (110-140 in pregnancy), mean cell volume 64 fL (80-100), mean cell haemoglobin 20 pg (27-33) and red cell count 5.6 x10^12/L (3.8-5.2), with ferritin 96 micrograms/L (15-200), normal C-reactive protein and normal B12 and folate. Her partner was born in Cyprus and has not been tested.

data_table.Examination: No pallor, no jaundice, no splenomegaly, uterus not palpable abdominally
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 103 g/L (110-140), mean cell volume 64 fL (80-100), mean cell haemoglobin 20 pg (27-33), red cell count 5.6 x10^12/L (3.8-5.2), ferritin 96 micrograms/L (15-200), C-reactive protein 2 mg/L (<5), B12 and folate within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request haemoglobin electrophoresis for her alone and test the partner only if hers is abnormal
options.rationale: Sequential testing is standard in many settings but costs weeks at exactly the point in pregnancy when chorionic villus sampling remains an option. The near-pair distinction from the correct approach is timing: with ancestry pointing to risk on both sides, parallel testing preserves the full range of reproductive choices. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal Screening and Diagnostic Testing)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal Screening and Diagnostic Testing

options.text: Request haemoglobin electrophoresis for her and arrange testing of her partner now
options.rationale: A ferritin of 96 micrograms/L with a normal C-reactive protein excludes iron deficiency as the cause of a mean cell volume of 64 fL, and a raised red cell count with disproportionate microcytosis is the classic thalassaemia trait picture. Because both partners have ancestry from high prevalence regions, partner testing must happen in parallel so that prenatal diagnosis remains available within the first trimester if both carry a variant. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal Screening and Diagnostic Testing)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal Screening and Diagnostic Testing

options.text: Request a blood film and reticulocyte count and defer further testing to the 28 week visit
options.rationale: A film showing target cells and basophilic stippling would support the suspicion but adds little to indices this characteristic, and reticulocytes do not discriminate. Deferring to 28 weeks removes every prenatal diagnostic option the couple might want. (Source: RANZCOG: Anaemia in Pregnancy)

options.text: Request non-invasive prenatal testing on maternal blood to assess the foetus for this condition
options.rationale: Non-invasive prenatal testing screens for common aneuploidies and does not detect haemoglobinopathies in routine Australian practice. Offering it here substitutes an unrelated screening test for carrier testing of the parents. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal Screening and Diagnostic Testing)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal Screening and Diagnostic Testing

options.text: Commence oral iron replacement and repeat the full blood count in four weeks to assess response
options.rationale: Her stores are replete, so giving iron cannot raise the haemoglobin and repeats the failed teenage trial she has already described. Continued supplementation in a thalassaemia carrier risks iron overload over time. (Source: RANZCOG: Anaemia in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Microcytic anaemia in pregnancy is so commonly due to iron deficiency that the diagnosis is often assumed, but ferritin with a concurrent C-reactive protein separates the two causes reliably, and a normal or high ferritin redirects the workup to haemoglobinopathy. Several features point that way here: the degree of microcytosis is out of proportion to the modest fall in haemoglobin, the red cell count is raised rather than reduced, the Mentzer index falls well below 13, and iron therapy previously failed. Beta thalassaemia trait carries little consequence for the woman herself, but if her partner also carries a beta variant each pregnancy has a one in four chance of transfusion-dependent beta thalassaemia major. That is why partner testing is urgent rather than routine, since chorionic villus sampling is available from around 11 weeks and amniocentesis from 15 weeks, and the counselling that precedes either takes time.
key_points: Ferritin with C-reactive protein distinguishes iron deficiency from thalassaemia trait
Disproportionate microcytosis with a raised red cell count suggests a haemoglobinopathy
Previous failure of iron therapy is a strong historical clue
Partner testing is urgent because prenatal diagnostic options are time limited
Alpha thalassaemia may need DNA studies because electrophoresis can be normal in carriers
explanation.pearls: The Mentzer index, the mean cell volume divided by the red cell count, is below 13 in thalassaemia trait and above 13 in iron deficiency, and here it is about 11, which flags the diagnosis from the full blood count alone before any specialised test is ordered.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Prenatal Screening and Diagnostic Testing

subtopic_detail: Duration criterion separating prolonged grief disorder from expected bereavement in an adult
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 58-year-old woman whose husband died of pancreatic cancer 19 months ago. She describes intense daily yearning for him, spends hours each day looking at his photographs and has kept his study exactly as he left it because moving anything feels like a betrayal.

She has stopped seeing the friends they shared because being with couples is unbearable, and says she does not know who she is without him. She sleeps reasonably, eats normally and has maintained her weight. She has no guilt beyond missing him, no anhedonia in activities unrelated to him, no psychomotor slowing and no thoughts of self harm. She has never had a psychiatric illness.

data_table.Examination: Well groomed, tearful when discussing her husband, reactive affect at other times, no psychomotor retardation, no psychotic features, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure her that this is a normal reaction to loss and review her again in six months
options.rationale: Grief that remains this intense and disabling beyond 12 months has crossed from an expected adaptation into a recognised disorder with its own treatment. Normalising it withholds an effective therapy and implies that continued suffering is simply to be endured. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Refer for a structured grief focused psychological therapy delivered over several months
options.rationale: Her symptoms have persisted beyond 12 months with identity disruption, avoidance of reminders and intense daily yearning causing functional impairment, which meets the threshold for prolonged grief disorder. Grief focused psychotherapy has the strongest evidence base for this condition and outperforms antidepressant monotherapy. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Suggest a community bereavement support group as the sole intervention for the next year
options.rationale: Peer support groups help many bereaved people and are a valuable adjunct, but they are not designed to treat a diagnosed disorder and have not shown efficacy for persistent grief of this severity. Offering only a group leaves the disorder untreated for another year. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Prescribe a short course of a benzodiazepine to help her tolerate the distressing memories
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines suppress the emotional processing that grief work depends on and carry dependence risk with prolonged use in this age group. Evidence suggests early benzodiazepine use after bereavement does not reduce and may prolong grief symptoms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence an antidepressant at standard dose and review the response in four weeks
options.rationale: She lacks the pervasive anhedonia, guilt, worthlessness and neurovegetative features that would indicate a depressive episode, and antidepressants have not been shown to reduce core grief symptoms. Medication has a place when major depression coexists, which it does not here. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: Prolonged grief disorder entered formal diagnostic classification to describe a minority of bereaved people whose grief does not attenuate and remains disabling long after the loss. The adult duration criterion is at least 12 months from the death, with the core features being persistent intense yearning or preoccupation with the deceased alongside identity disruption, disbelief, avoidance of reminders, emotional numbness, a sense of meaninglessness and difficulty re-engaging with life. The distinction from major depression matters because the sadness in grief is focused on the lost person and comes in waves triggered by reminders, while depressive mood is pervasive and accompanied by global worthlessness and anhedonia. Treatment is psychological first, with grief focused cognitive behavioural approaches producing the largest effects, and medication reserved for comorbid depression or anxiety.
key_points: The adult duration criterion for prolonged grief disorder is at least 12 months after the death
Core features are intense yearning or preoccupation with identity disruption and avoidance
Grief sadness is focused on the deceased and comes in waves; depressive mood is pervasive
Grief focused psychotherapy outperforms antidepressants for core grief symptoms
Treat comorbid major depression or post traumatic stress disorder on their own merits
explanation.pearls: The duration criterion is 12 months in adults but only 6 months in children and adolescents, so a bereaved teenager with disabling grief at 8 months meets the diagnosis while an adult with the same picture at the same interval does not yet.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: Scheduled analgesic trial for agitation in advanced dementia with no verbal pain report
stem:
You are the general practitioner attending a residential aged care facility to review an 84-year-old woman with advanced Alzheimer disease who has become resistive and strikes out during personal care, particularly when staff transfer her or dress her upper body. Her speech is limited to occasional single words.

Staff report the behaviour has built over three weeks and occurs mainly during morning cares rather than at any particular time of day. She has severe knee osteoarthritis and fell onto her right shoulder six weeks ago, after which a radiograph showed no fracture. She takes no regular analgesia. Urinalysis, full blood count, electrolytes, calcium and a chest radiograph performed this week are all unremarkable, and there has been no medication change.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78/min, blood pressure 132/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.6 C
data_table.Examination: Grimaces and pulls away on passive right shoulder abduction, crepitus in both knees, abdomen soft, no urinary retention on bladder scan, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative, full blood count, electrolytes, corrected calcium and C-reactive protein within normal limits, chest radiograph clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence low dose risperidone and review the behaviour after several weeks of treatment
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are considered only after reversible causes and non-pharmacological approaches have failed, and they raise the risk of stroke and death in older people with dementia. Starting one before treating obvious untreated pain exposes her to that risk for a problem that has a safer remedy. (Source: RANZCP: Antipsychotics in Dementia Position Statement)
source_refs: RANZCP: Antipsychotics in Dementia Position Statement

options.text: Commence a low dose antidepressant for presumed depression underlying the behaviour change
options.rationale: Depression can present as agitation in dementia and citalopram has some evidence in this setting, but the behaviour here is tightly bound to physical handling rather than pervasive across the day. The pattern points to a nociceptive trigger rather than a mood disturbance. (Source: RACGP: Aged Care Clinical Guide)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the right shoulder before making any treatment change
options.rationale: A rotator cuff tear is plausible and imaging might confirm it, but scanning a woman with advanced dementia requires her to lie still for a prolonged period and rarely changes management at this stage. An empirical analgesic trial tests the same hypothesis without the burden. (Source: RACGP: Aged Care Clinical Guide)

options.text: Arrange an as-required oral benzodiazepine for staff to give before morning personal cares
options.rationale: Pre-medicating with a benzodiazepine sedates her through a painful experience rather than removing the pain, and increases falls, confusion and aspiration risk. As-required sedation before care is a form of chemical restraint when a treatable cause has not been addressed. (Source: RANZCP: Antipsychotics in Dementia Position Statement)
source_refs: RANZCP: Antipsychotics in Dementia Position Statement

options.text: Commence regular scheduled paracetamol and reassess the behaviour after several weeks
options.rationale: Untreated pain is among the commonest reversible drivers of behavioural change in advanced dementia, and a person who cannot report it communicates through resistance during the movements that hurt. A stepwise trial of regular rather than as-required simple analgesia has been shown in randomised trials to reduce agitation substantially. (Source: RACGP: Aged Care Clinical Guide)

explanation.summary: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia are best understood as communication rather than as symptoms requiring suppression, and the first task is always to look for an unmet need. Pain, constipation, urinary retention, infection, delirium, sensory impairment, boredom, fear and an over-stimulating environment account for a large share of behaviour that would otherwise be medicated. Pain is particularly easy to miss because the standard question cannot be answered, so assessment relies on observational tools and on the pattern of when the behaviour occurs, with resistance confined to handling being highly suggestive. Randomised evidence supports a stepwise protocol beginning with regular paracetamol, and antipsychotics carry a well-quantified increase in cerebrovascular events and mortality that makes them a last rather than a first resort.
key_points: Behaviour in dementia is communication; look for an unmet need before prescribing
Pain, constipation, retention, infection and delirium are the commonest reversible drivers
Behaviour confined to personal care or movement strongly suggests pain
A stepwise trial of regular paracetamol reduces agitation in randomised trials
Antipsychotics increase stroke and mortality risk in older people with dementia
explanation.pearls: When an antipsychotic is unavoidable in dementia, risperidone is the only agent with an Australian indication for persistent aggression, at a starting dose of 0.25 mg twice daily, and the approved duration is up to 12 weeks with review for withdrawal at that point.

sources.label: RANZCP: Antipsychotics in Dementia Position Statement

subtopic_detail: Baseline cardiovascular assessment required before starting stimulant treatment in an adult
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in the adult outpatient clinic having completed a diagnostic assessment of a 28-year-old man with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, combined presentation, with a documented history of symptoms from primary school and current impairment at work and at home.

He drinks alcohol twice a week within recommended limits and uses no other substances. He has no history of psychosis, mania or tics. His mother has a pacemaker for complete heart block diagnosed in her sixties and there is no family history of sudden death under 40. He is otherwise well and takes no regular medication. You plan to start a long acting methylphenidate preparation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74/min, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, heart sounds dual with no murmur, chest clear, no tremor, no thyroid enlargement

lead_in: What baseline assessment is most important before the first prescription?

options.text: Record pulse, blood pressure, weight and a cardiovascular and family cardiac history
options.rationale: Stimulants raise heart rate and blood pressure modestly in most people, so a documented baseline is what makes subsequent monitoring interpretable, alongside a structured cardiac history to identify who needs further investigation. Australian guidance treats this clinical assessment rather than routine investigation as the required baseline. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Arrange formal neuropsychological testing to confirm the diagnosis before treatment starts
options.rationale: Neuropsychological testing cannot diagnose or exclude this condition, which remains a clinical diagnosis based on history, developmental course and corroborative information. It is useful for characterising a suspected specific learning disorder alongside it. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Arrange urine drug screening and repeat it at every review while treatment continues
options.rationale: Substance use history is an important part of the assessment and influences the choice of preparation, but universal repeated urine screening is not recommended and damages the therapeutic relationship. He reports alcohol within limits and no other substance use. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Arrange a twelve lead electrocardiogram for every adult before any stimulant is commenced
options.rationale: Routine electrocardiography for all patients is not recommended because the yield in people without cardiac symptoms or a concerning family history is very low. It is indicated when the history reveals structural disease, exertional syncope, palpitations or premature sudden death in a relative. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Arrange transthoracic echocardiography given the family history of conduction system disease
options.rationale: Acquired heart block in a woman in her sixties is age related and does not indicate an inherited cardiomyopathy or channelopathy in her son. Echocardiography is reserved for a murmur, symptoms or a family history of cardiomyopathy or premature sudden death. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

explanation.summary: Stimulant medication is the most effective treatment for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in adults, with effect sizes that exceed most interventions in psychiatry, and the safety framework around it is built on simple repeated clinical measurement rather than on investigation. The relevant physiological effects are a small rise in heart rate and blood pressure, appetite suppression with weight loss, and sleep disruption if dosing runs late in the day. Baseline pulse, blood pressure and weight are recorded so that change can be detected, and the cardiac history is taken to identify the small group with structural or electrical disease in whom a cardiology opinion is needed first. In Australia stimulant prescribing is regulated at state and territory level with authority requirements, and driving must be discussed because untreated symptoms themselves raise crash risk while treatment reduces it.
key_points: Baseline pulse, blood pressure and weight make later monitoring interpretable
Routine electrocardiography is not required in the absence of cardiac symptoms or family red flags
Red flags include exertional syncope, palpitations, structural disease and sudden death under 40 in a relative
Neuropsychological testing cannot confirm or exclude the diagnosis
Stimulant prescribing in Australia requires state or territory authority
explanation.pearls: Treating adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder reduces motor vehicle crash risk rather than increasing it, and long acting preparations are preferred for drivers because the wearing-off period of short acting formulations produces a rebound window of impaired attention in the late afternoon.

sources.label: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

subtopic_detail: Choosing between psychological therapy and medication as initial treatment for uncomplicated adult PTSD
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34-year-old paramedic who attended a multi-fatality road crash seven months ago. Since then he has had nightly nightmares, intrusive images of the scene when he hears sirens, and he has changed his driving route to avoid the intersection.

He has become irritable with his partner, sleeps four to five hours a night and startles at unexpected noises. He has reduced his shifts and describes feeling permanently on edge. He drinks two standard drinks most evenings, which has not changed. He has no psychotic symptoms, no history of mania and no thoughts of suicide, and he has never had psychiatric treatment.

data_table.Examination: Anxious but engaged, no psychomotor agitation, affect reactive, cognition intact, no psychotic phenomena, insight preserved
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Advise a period of sick leave with sleep hygiene measures and review him in two months
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is appropriate in the first month after trauma when many people recover spontaneously, but symptoms established at seven months will not remit with rest alone. Extended avoidance of work can reinforce the avoidance that maintains the disorder. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Commence a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review his response in four weeks
options.rationale: Medication is recommended when trauma focused therapy is declined, unavailable or ineffective, or when there is significant comorbid depression, none of which applies. Starting with a drug when therapy is accessible inverts the recommended order. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Arrange a single session psychological debriefing focused on the details of the incident
options.rationale: Single session debriefing is not recommended at any stage and evidence suggests it can worsen outcomes by reactivating distress without providing the structured processing that therapy offers. It is also seven months too late to be conceived of as an early intervention. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Refer for individual trauma focused cognitive behavioural therapy with a trained therapist
options.rationale: Australian guidelines recommend trauma focused psychological therapy as first line for adult post traumatic stress disorder, with larger effect sizes and better maintenance of gains after treatment ends than medication. Eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing is an equally recommended alternative within this first line group. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Prescribe prazosin at night as the initial treatment directed at his nightmares and sleep
options.rationale: Prazosin has a genuine role as an adjunct for trauma related nightmares that persist despite first line treatment, and would be considered later. Using it alone leaves the intrusions, avoidance and hyperarousal that define the disorder untreated. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Post traumatic stress disorder requires exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence, followed by symptoms in four clusters: intrusion, avoidance, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and alterations in arousal and reactivity, persisting beyond one month with functional impairment. Occupational exposure is explicitly included, which is why emergency service workers carry elevated rates. The treatment hierarchy is unusually clear in this condition: trauma focused psychological therapies, principally trauma focused cognitive behavioural therapy and eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing, outperform pharmacotherapy and their benefits persist better after treatment stops. Medication is the second line option or an adjunct where comorbidity demands it, and benzodiazepines are specifically discouraged because they impair the extinction learning that therapy relies on.
key_points: Trauma focused cognitive behavioural therapy and eye movement desensitisation are first line
Medication is second line or reserved for comorbid depression or when therapy is unavailable
Single session debriefing is not recommended and may cause harm
Benzodiazepines impair extinction learning and should be avoided
Prazosin is an adjunct for persistent trauma related nightmares
explanation.pearls: Symptoms lasting between 3 days and 1 month after the event constitute acute stress disorder rather than post traumatic stress disorder, and the practical significance is that around half of people with acute stress disorder do not go on to develop the chronic condition.

subtopic_detail: Evaluating new behaviour change in an adult with intellectual disability before attributing it to the disability
stem:
You are the general practitioner asked to see a 32-year-old man with moderate intellectual disability who lives in supported accommodation. Over the past six weeks he has begun hitting the side of his head with his palm and refusing meals he previously enjoyed, and staff describe him as withdrawn from activities he used to seek out.

He communicates with around 40 signs and single words and has never described pain in words. There has been no change in staffing, housemates, routine or medication, and no recent bereavement or family visit change. Staff have requested a referral to a psychiatrist for an antipsychotic because they believe the behaviour is part of his disability.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88/min, blood pressure 126/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Reluctant to allow examination of the head and neck, no external ear discharge, no obvious dental abnormality visible on limited inspection, abdomen soft, gait unchanged

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor for a presumed underlying depressive illness
options.rationale: Depression does present atypically in intellectual disability, with irritability, withdrawal and loss of skills rather than a verbal account of low mood, so it remains on the differential. Treating it empirically before excluding physical illness risks a months-long trial while a dental abscess goes untreated. (Source: RANZCP: Intellectual Disability Mental Health Position Statement)
source_refs: RANZCP: Intellectual Disability Mental Health Position Statement

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the brain to exclude an intracranial cause for the behaviour
options.rationale: Neuroimaging is indicated if there are new neurological signs, seizures or a fall with head injury, none of which is present. Jumping to a scan skips the far higher yield examinations of the teeth, ears and abdomen that the behaviour is pointing towards. (Source: RACGP: Health Care of People with Intellectual Disability)
source_refs: RACGP: Health Care of People with Intellectual Disability

options.text: Undertake a systematic search for a physical cause including dental, ear and gastrointestinal review
options.rationale: New behaviour of this kind in a person with limited verbal communication is most often the expression of a physical problem, with dental disease, otitis, reflux, constipation and musculoskeletal pain heading the list. Attributing it to the intellectual disability itself is diagnostic overshadowing, the best documented source of avoidable harm in this population. (Source: RANZCP: Intellectual Disability Mental Health Position Statement)
source_refs: RANZCP: Intellectual Disability Mental Health Position Statement

options.text: Advise staff to implement a behaviour support plan using planned ignoring of the behaviour
options.rationale: A positive behaviour support plan is a legitimate and often essential intervention, but it must be built on a functional assessment that has first excluded pain and illness. Planned ignoring of head striking driven by ear or dental pain leaves the person in pain and unheard. (Source: RANZCP: Intellectual Disability Mental Health Position Statement)
source_refs: RANZCP: Intellectual Disability Mental Health Position Statement

options.text: Refer to psychiatry for antipsychotic treatment of the self injurious behaviour as requested
options.rationale: Psychotropic medication is widely overprescribed in this population for behaviour that has an untreated physical or environmental cause, and it brings metabolic, extrapyramidal and sedative harms. A psychiatric referral may be warranted later but not before physical causes are excluded. (Source: RANZCP: Intellectual Disability Mental Health Position Statement)
source_refs: RANZCP: Intellectual Disability Mental Health Position Statement

explanation.summary: People with intellectual disability have substantially higher rates of untreated physical illness and a markedly lower life expectancy than the general population, and diagnostic overshadowing is a principal driver of that gap. The term describes the error of attributing new symptoms or behaviour to the disability itself rather than investigating them as one would in anyone else. Behaviour change is the presenting complaint for conditions that would otherwise be described verbally, so the differential begins with pain from teeth, ears, joints and abdomen, and includes constipation, reflux, urinary infection, epilepsy, sensory loss and medication adverse effects. Once physical causes are excluded, a functional behavioural assessment examines environmental triggers and communicative intent, and psychiatric diagnosis and medication follow only after those two steps.
key_points: Diagnostic overshadowing means wrongly attributing new symptoms to the intellectual disability
Behaviour change is often the only available expression of pain or illness
Dental disease, otitis, constipation, reflux and musculoskeletal pain are high yield
Functional behavioural assessment follows exclusion of physical causes
Psychotropic medication is overprescribed in this population and needs regular review
explanation.pearls: Annual comprehensive health assessment for adults with intellectual disability is supported by a dedicated Medicare item in Australia and reliably uncovers unrecognised problems such as untreated hearing loss, vision impairment and chronic constipation that commonly present first as behaviour change.

sources.label: RANZCP: Intellectual Disability Mental Health Position Statement
RACGP: Health Care of People with Intellectual Disability

subtopic_detail: Reconsidering an existing personality disorder label when an adult woman describes lifelong autistic traits
stem:
