You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 29-year-old woman diagnosed with borderline personality disorder at 21 who has completed two full dialectical behaviour therapy programmes with little change. She was referred again after a further period of distress following a workplace restructure.

She describes her overwhelming distress as consistently triggered by unexpected changes to plans, by open plan office noise and by fluorescent lighting rather than by interpersonal rejection. Her relationships have been few but stable, and she denies frantic efforts to avoid abandonment or a chronically unstable sense of self. Her self harm has always been in response to sensory or change-related overload. She reports rehearsing conversations in advance, and her mother says she lined up her toys in strict order and taught herself to copy other girls' social behaviour at school.

data_table.Examination: Limited eye contact, precise and formal speech, no thought disorder, no psychotic features, mood euthymic today, cognition intact, wears noise cancelling headphones into the consultation
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Focus treatment on the workplace restructure and refer for supportive counselling and return to work
options.rationale: The restructure is the precipitant that brought her back but not the reason two evidence-based treatment courses have failed over eight years. Treating only the trigger leaves the diagnostic question and the sensory environment that generates her distress unaddressed. (Source: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia)
source_refs: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia

options.text: Refer for a structured multidisciplinary adult autism diagnostic assessment with developmental history
options.rationale: Her distress is triggered by change and sensory input rather than by abandonment, her relationships and identity are stable, and the developmental history describes restricted interests and learned social camouflaging. Autistic women are frequently misdiagnosed with borderline personality disorder, and a formal reassessment reframes both the diagnosis and what support will actually help. (Source: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia)
source_refs: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia

options.text: Refer her for a third course of dialectical behaviour therapy with a different treating team
options.rationale: Two adequate courses without benefit is evidence that the formulation rather than the therapist is wrong, and repeating a treatment aimed at abandonment sensitivity and identity disturbance will not address sensory and change intolerance. Some skills modules may still help, but as part of a revised formulation. (Source: RANZCP: Personality Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Personality Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Commence a mood stabiliser to reduce affective instability while continuing her current therapy
options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy has a limited evidence base in borderline personality disorder and is recommended only for comorbid conditions or short term crisis management. Adding a drug to an unexamined diagnosis treats a symptom label rather than the underlying problem. (Source: RANZCP: Personality Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Personality Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Administer a self report autism screening questionnaire and make the diagnosis if she scores highly
options.rationale: Screening instruments have a useful role in deciding who to refer but cannot establish the diagnosis, which requires developmental history, collateral information and direct observation across domains. The near-pair distinction from the correct approach is screening versus diagnostic assessment. (Source: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia)
source_refs: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia

explanation.summary: Autism is diagnosed considerably later in women and girls than in men and boys, and a substantial proportion receive a psychiatric label first, most often borderline personality disorder, an eating disorder or an anxiety disorder. The reason is camouflaging, the effortful learning and rehearsal of social behaviour that masks the underlying difficulty at enormous cognitive and emotional cost, which makes the presentation diverge from the male-derived stereotype that most clinicians pattern match against. Several features help discriminate the two diagnoses: in autism the distress is triggered by sensory overload and unpredictability rather than by perceived rejection, identity is stable rather than diffuse, relationships are few but not characterised by idealisation and devaluation, and the traits are lifelong and pervasive rather than emerging in adolescence. Getting this right changes everything downstream, because the useful interventions become sensory and environmental accommodation, predictability and communication support rather than emotion regulation therapy.
key_points: Autistic women are commonly misdiagnosed with borderline personality disorder
Camouflaging masks the presentation and delays diagnosis in women and girls
Autistic distress follows sensory overload and unexpected change rather than abandonment
Identity and relationship patterns are stable in autism and unstable in borderline personality disorder
Diagnosis requires developmental history and collateral information, not a screening score
explanation.pearls: Autistic burnout, presenting as profound exhaustion, loss of previously held skills and reduced tolerance of sensory input after a period of sustained camouflaging, is frequently mistaken for a depressive episode, and it responds to reduced demand and sensory recovery rather than to antidepressants.

sources.label: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia
RANZCP: Personality Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: Neuroleptic sensitivity constraining treatment of visual hallucinations in Lewy body disease
stem:
You are the geriatric medicine registrar reviewing a 76-year-old man whose wife reports that for the past four months he has seen small children standing in the corner of the lounge room in the late afternoon, and has spoken to them. He knows afterwards that they were not there.

She also describes days when he is lucid and days when he stares vacantly for hours, and says he has acted out dreams and struck her while asleep for several years. He has had two falls in three months. On examination there is mild symmetrical bradykinesia and increased tone in both arms with no resting tremor. His Montreal Cognitive Assessment score is 21 out of 30 with prominent deficits in attention and visuospatial tasks. Screening for infection, electrolyte disturbance and hypothyroidism is negative and he takes no anticholinergic medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72/min, blood pressure 138/80 mmHg lying and 108/64 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Symmetrical bradykinesia and increased tone in both upper limbs, no resting tremor, Montreal Cognitive Assessment 21/30 with attentional and visuospatial deficits, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, calcium, thyroid function and urinalysis within normal limits, computed tomography of the brain shows generalised atrophy only

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of his hallucinations?

options.text: Commence rivastigmine after explaining that hallucinations often improve with this treatment
options.rationale: Fluctuating cognition, well formed visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and a history of dream enactment describe dementia with Lewy bodies, in which the cholinergic deficit is more profound than in Alzheimer disease. Cholinesterase inhibitors improve both cognition and the visual hallucinations in this condition and avoid the dopamine blockade that these patients tolerate so poorly. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and Management of Dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and Management of Dementia

options.text: Commence low dose haloperidol at night with review of the hallucinations after two weeks
options.rationale: Severe neuroleptic sensitivity reactions occur in up to half of these patients and can produce irreversible parkinsonism, autonomic instability and death, with high potency typical agents carrying the greatest risk. This is the single most dangerous prescription in this diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and Management of Dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and Management of Dementia

options.text: Commence levodopa with carbidopa to address the parkinsonism and the associated hallucinations
options.rationale: Levodopa is used cautiously for disabling parkinsonism in this condition but characteristically worsens hallucinations by increasing dopaminergic tone. Using it to treat the hallucinations targets the right patient with exactly the wrong direction of effect. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and Management of Dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and Management of Dementia

options.text: Commence a regular night time benzodiazepine to reduce the dream enactment and the hallucinations
options.rationale: Clonazepam and melatonin are both used for rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder, but a benzodiazepine in a man with postural hypotension and two recent falls compounds his greatest immediate risk. It also does nothing for daytime visual hallucinations. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence low dose risperidone at night with review of the hallucinations after two weeks
options.rationale: Risperidone has meaningful dopamine D2 blockade at therapeutic doses and carries the same neuroleptic sensitivity risk as a typical agent in this population. The near-pair distinction from a safer choice is the degree of D2 antagonism rather than whether the drug is labelled atypical. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and Management of Dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and Management of Dementia

explanation.summary: Dementia with Lewy bodies is the second commonest neurodegenerative dementia and is defined by a core clinical triad of fluctuating cognition with pronounced variation in attention and alertness, recurrent well formed visual hallucinations, and spontaneous parkinsonism, with rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder as a fourth core feature that often precedes the others by years. The cognitive profile is distinguishable from Alzheimer disease by early attentional, executive and visuospatial impairment with relative preservation of memory. Autonomic dysfunction, particularly orthostatic hypotension, contributes heavily to the falls burden. The defining management constraint is neuroleptic sensitivity, a severe and sometimes fatal reaction to dopamine antagonists, which means that any antipsychotic is a last resort and that quetiapine or clozapine are the only agents contemplated when one is unavoidable.
key_points: Core features are fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and dream enactment
Cholinesterase inhibitors improve cognition and reduce hallucinations in this dementia
Neuroleptic sensitivity affects up to half of patients and can be fatal
Risperidone and haloperidol are both hazardous; quetiapine or clozapine only if unavoidable
Orthostatic hypotension is common and drives falls
explanation.pearls: The one year rule separates dementia with Lewy bodies from Parkinson disease dementia: cognitive decline beginning before or within 12 months of the onset of parkinsonism indicates the former, while dementia arising years after established Parkinson disease indicates the latter, though the treatment constraints are identical.

sources.label: RANZCP: Assessment and Management of Dementia

subtopic_detail: Supervised administration and observation requirements when starting intranasal esketamine
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar planning treatment for a 44-year-old woman with a major depressive episode that has failed adequate trials of three antidepressants from two classes and an augmentation trial, each at therapeutic dose for at least six weeks with confirmed adherence.

She has no psychotic features, no history of mania and no substance use disorder. Her blood pressure is 138/86 mmHg on repeated readings and she has no history of aneurysm, arteriovenous malformation or intracerebral haemorrhage. She lives alone, drives herself to appointments and works part time. The team has agreed to proceed with intranasal esketamine alongside her oral antidepressant.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76/min, blood pressure 138/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 C
data_table.Examination: Depressed affect, no psychotic features, no psychomotor retardation, cognition intact, no thoughts of self harm today
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: Which arrangement is essential for the first dose?

options.text: Cease her oral antidepressant before the first dose to avoid a serotonergic drug interaction
options.rationale: Esketamine is licensed for use in combination with an oral antidepressant rather than as monotherapy, and the pivotal trials were conducted with that combination. Stopping the antidepressant removes part of the treatment and risks discontinuation symptoms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance angiography of the cerebral vessels before the first dose is given
options.rationale: Vascular imaging is not a routine requirement, and aneurysmal or arteriovenous disease is excluded by history and examination in the absence of red flags. She has already been screened clinically and found to have none. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Dispense it for home administration with a telephone review on the evening of each dose
options.rationale: Home administration is not permitted for this medicine in Australia precisely because dissociation and haemodynamic change occur predictably in the observation window. A telephone call cannot substitute for direct observation and blood pressure measurement. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Administer it in a supervised healthcare setting with blood pressure checks and prolonged observation
options.rationale: Esketamine causes dissociation, sedation and a transient blood pressure rise peaking in the first 40 minutes, so every dose is self administered under direct supervision with blood pressure measured before and after and observation continuing for at least two hours until the patient is clinically stable. She must also be told not to drive until the following day after restful sleep. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Admit her as an inpatient for the full induction course of twice weekly dosing over four weeks
options.rationale: Inpatient admission is required only when the clinical situation demands it, such as high suicide risk or significant comorbidity, and routine induction is delivered in a supervised outpatient clinic. Hospitalising every patient would be disproportionate and would limit access. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Treatment resistant depression is conventionally defined as failure to respond to two or more adequate trials of antidepressants of adequate dose and duration in the current episode, and before escalating it is essential to confirm the diagnosis, adherence, dose adequacy and the absence of a bipolar diathesis or an unrecognised medical or substance contributor. Esketamine acts through N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor antagonism and downstream glutamatergic and synaptogenic effects rather than through monoamine reuptake, which is why it can produce benefit within hours to days where conventional agents take weeks. That speed comes with a distinctive acute adverse effect profile of dissociation, sedation, dizziness, nausea and transient blood pressure elevation, all of which cluster in the first 90 minutes. The resulting requirement for supervised administration and post-dose observation shapes the entire service model, and the alternatives at this point in the treatment ladder remain electroconvulsive therapy, augmentation strategies and transcranial magnetic stimulation.
key_points: Esketamine is self administered under direct supervision in a healthcare setting, never at home
Blood pressure is measured before dosing and after, with observation for at least two hours
It is used in combination with an oral antidepressant rather than as monotherapy
Patients must not drive until the day after the dose following restful sleep
Dissociation, sedation and transient hypertension peak within the first 40 minutes
explanation.pearls: A history of aneurysmal vascular disease, arteriovenous malformation or intracerebral haemorrhage is a contraindication to esketamine because the transient blood pressure rise of around 10 to 15 mmHg systolic peaks at roughly 40 minutes after dosing and could precipitate rupture.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: Sequencing stabilisation before memory processing in prolonged repeated childhood trauma
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 37-year-old woman referred for trauma therapy after disclosing repeated sexual abuse between the ages of 6 and 13 by a family member. She has intrusive memories, avoidance and hyperarousal.

She also describes losing periods of time, sometimes arriving somewhere with no memory of travelling there, and a persistent sense of being detached from her own body. She has cut herself several times in the past two months when distressed and has been admitted twice this year after overdoses. She struggles to name emotions and says she either feels nothing or feels everything at once. She has stable housing and no substance use disorder.

data_table.Examination: Appears detached during parts of the interview with delayed responses, no psychotic features, oriented, no current suicidal intent though reports intermittent urges, healed and recent superficial forearm lacerations
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial phase of treatment?

options.text: Begin eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing targeting the earliest abuse memory first
options.rationale: This modality is first line for post traumatic stress disorder and will very likely form part of her later treatment, but its processing phases carry the same destabilisation risk as exposure in this context. The near-pair distinction from the correct answer is the phase of treatment rather than the modality chosen. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Defer all psychological treatment and commence an antidepressant with review in eight weeks
options.rationale: Medication may help comorbid depression but does not treat the trauma or the dissociation, and deferring psychological work entirely leaves her without the skills she most needs. Stabilisation is psychological treatment, not a delay before it. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Begin prolonged exposure therapy immediately with detailed recounting of the abuse memories
options.rationale: Exposure is highly effective for single incident trauma in a person with intact regulation, but starting it during active dissociation and recent overdoses risks escalating self harm and dropout. The issue is sequencing rather than whether exposure is ever appropriate for her. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Begin with stabilisation focused on safety, emotion regulation and grounding skills
options.rationale: Australian guidelines recommend a phased approach for complex presentations with prolonged repeated trauma, significant dissociation and recent self harm, because memory processing without regulation capacity can precipitate decompensation and increase risk. Stabilisation builds the affect tolerance and grounding skills that make later trauma processing survivable and effective. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian PTSD Guidelines)

options.text: Arrange inpatient admission for the duration of trauma processing to manage the self harm risk
options.rationale: Prolonged admission for people with chronic self harm and complex trauma is generally counterproductive, tending to reinforce crisis presentations and erode autonomy. Brief admission has a place for acute risk, but not as the setting for a course of trauma therapy. (Source: RANZCP: Personality Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Personality Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: Trauma that is prolonged, repeated and inflicted in childhood by a caregiver produces a presentation that extends beyond the classical intrusion, avoidance and hyperarousal clusters to include difficulties with affect regulation, a persistently negative self concept and impaired relationships, described in the international classification as complex post traumatic stress disorder. Dissociation sits at the centre of the clinical problem, ranging from depersonalisation and derealisation to amnesic gaps, and it both arises as a protective response and interferes with the processing that therapy requires. Australian guidance therefore recommends a phased model in which stabilisation precedes memory processing, which in turn precedes reintegration, with the length of the first phase determined by the person's regulation capacity rather than by a fixed schedule. The common error runs in both directions: processing too early destabilises, while stabilising indefinitely means the trauma is never addressed.
key_points: Complex presentations add affect dysregulation, negative self concept and relational difficulty
A phased approach places stabilisation before memory processing and then reintegration
Dissociation and active self harm are indications to extend the stabilisation phase
Trauma focused therapies remain the goal rather than being abandoned
Indefinite stabilisation without ever processing trauma is also a treatment failure
explanation.pearls: Dissociation during a therapy session is managed with grounding through the five senses rather than by continuing to process the memory, because material encoded while the person is dissociated is not integrated and the session reinforces avoidance instead of extinction.

sources.label: RANZCP: Personality Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: Choosing a non-stimulant for attention deficit disorder when methamphetamine use is ongoing
stem:
You are the addiction psychiatry registrar seeing a 26-year-old man attending a community drug and alcohol service. He has a well documented childhood diagnosis of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder treated with stimulants until he was 15, when he stopped medication and left school.

He has used methamphetamine three or four times a week for the past four years, most recently two days ago. He describes longstanding inattention, disorganisation and impulsivity that were present well before he began using, and that persist during his longest abstinent period of five months last year. He has no psychotic symptoms currently, though he had brief paranoia during a heavy use episode last year that resolved within a week of stopping. He wants treatment for his attention problems and is engaged with a case manager.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88/min, blood pressure 132/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Alert, restless in the chair, no psychotic phenomena, no tremor, dentition poor, cognition grossly intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes and liver function within normal limits, urine drug screen positive for amfetamine type substances, electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with normal intervals

lead_in: Which pharmacological treatment would you recommend?

options.text: Bupropion commenced at low dose with gradual increase and review of the response in six weeks
options.rationale: Bupropion has modest evidence in adults with this condition and is sometimes used for concurrent nicotine dependence, but it is not a recommended first line agent. It also lowers the seizure threshold, which matters in someone using stimulants heavily. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Defer all pharmacological treatment until he has achieved twelve months of confirmed abstinence
options.rationale: Requiring prolonged abstinence before treating an untreated neurodevelopmental disorder is a common but counterproductive stance, since impulsivity and inattention themselves undermine the capacity to stop using. Effective treatment of the disorder supports rather than competes with substance use treatment. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Long acting methylphenidate dispensed daily with supervised dosing at a community pharmacy
options.rationale: A long acting preparation with supervised dosing is the reasonable stimulant option once substance use is stable or abstinent, and it may well become appropriate for him later. Starting it while he is using several times a week places the prescriber in the position of supplying a stimulant to someone actively using one. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Atomoxetine titrated gradually with review of the response after six to eight weeks
options.rationale: A non-stimulant with no misuse or diversion potential is preferred while stimulant use is active, and atomoxetine has the best evidence base among the non-stimulants for adults with this comorbidity. Its effect builds over weeks rather than within hours, which also removes the reinforcing immediate reward that complicates stimulant use. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.text: Immediate release dexamfetamine dispensed weekly with review of the response after six weeks
options.rationale: An immediate release stimulant during active methamphetamine use carries the highest risk of misuse and diversion of any option, and weekly dispensing does not remove that risk. Short acting preparations are the least suitable stimulant formulation in this setting. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

explanation.summary: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and substance use disorders co-occur far more often than chance, and the relationship runs in both directions: impulsivity and reward sensitivity raise the likelihood of early substance use, while untreated symptoms make sustained abstinence harder. The diagnostic challenge is distinguishing the disorder from the cognitive effects of chronic stimulant use, and the evidence that settles it here is a documented childhood diagnosis with symptoms persisting through a five month abstinent period. Australian guidance supports treating both conditions concurrently rather than sequentially, since withholding treatment until abstinence is achieved commonly means never treating at all. Where stimulant use is active, a non-stimulant avoids the prescriber contributing to the problem, and stimulants can be revisited with long acting preparations and supervised dosing once use is stable.
key_points: Treat the neurodevelopmental disorder and the substance use disorder concurrently, not sequentially
Symptoms persisting during abstinence support a primary diagnosis rather than drug effect
Non-stimulants are preferred while stimulant use is active
Atomoxetine takes six to eight weeks for full effect, unlike the immediate effect of stimulants
Long acting formulations with supervised dosing are the safer stimulant option later
explanation.pearls: Atomoxetine carries a specific warning for hepatotoxicity, so unexplained nausea with right upper quadrant pain, dark urine or jaundice during treatment requires immediate cessation and liver function testing rather than dose reduction.

sources.label: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

subtopic_detail: Benzodiazepine challenge when immobility is attributed to a severe depressive episode
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to see a 23-year-old woman on a medical ward, admitted three days ago for poor oral intake. She has a six week history of low mood and social withdrawal and the admitting team has diagnosed a severe depressive episode with psychomotor retardation.

She has spoken four words in three days and lies still with her eyes open. When you lift her arm above the bed it remains where you place it for over a minute. She resists passive neck flexion with equal opposing force, and repeats the last words of your questions back to you. She is afebrile with no rigidity, and there has been no antipsychotic exposure. Creatine kinase is 420 U/L (30-200), white cell count, electrolytes, calcium, thyroid function and a computed tomography scan of the brain are all unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92/min, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Maintains imposed postures for over a minute, opposes passive movement with equal force, echolalia present, no lead pipe rigidity, no tremor, no clonus, no autonomic instability
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 420 U/L (30-200), white cell count, electrolytes, corrected calcium and thyroid function within normal limits, computed tomography of the brain unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange urgent electroencephalography to exclude non-convulsive status epilepticus as the cause
options.rationale: Non-convulsive status is a genuine differential for an unresponsive patient and electroencephalography is worth obtaining, but waxy flexibility and gegenhalten are specific motor signs that point strongly to catatonia. The benzodiazepine challenge is faster and would improve both conditions if either were present. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Commence an antipsychotic to treat the presumed psychotic component of the depressive episode
options.rationale: Dopamine antagonists can precipitate malignant catatonia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome in a patient who is already catatonic, making this the most dangerous available choice. Antipsychotics are withheld until the catatonia has resolved. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Refer directly for electroconvulsive therapy without any preceding pharmacological trial
options.rationale: Electroconvulsive therapy is the definitive treatment for catatonia and is indicated when the benzodiazepine trial fails or when malignant features are present, and it may still be needed here. Bypassing a trial that resolves most cases within hours and requires no anaesthetic is not the proportionate first step. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Commence an antidepressant and arrange nasogastric feeding while awaiting the treatment response
options.rationale: Nutrition and hydration do need urgent attention, but an antidepressant takes weeks and does not treat catatonia, leaving her immobile and at risk of venous thromboembolism, pressure injury and aspiration meanwhile. Supportive care is necessary but is not the treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Administer a parenteral lorazepam challenge and assess the clinical response within minutes
options.rationale: Waxy flexibility, gegenhalten, mutism, immobility and echolalia constitute catatonia rather than psychomotor retardation, and a benzodiazepine challenge is both the diagnostic test and the start of treatment, with a marked response within 10 to 30 minutes in most cases. Recognising it matters because catatonia can progress to the malignant form with autonomic instability, rhabdomyolysis and death. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a syndrome of motor dysregulation that occurs across mood disorders, psychotic disorders and a wide range of medical and neurological conditions, and mood disorders are in fact its commonest psychiatric context. It is systematically underdiagnosed because its features are misread as severe depression, as negativism, or as a general medical deterioration, and the specific signs that distinguish it are motor rather than affective: waxy flexibility, catalepsy, gegenhalten, posturing, mutism, negativism, stereotypy, echolalia and echopraxia. The benzodiazepine challenge occupies an unusual position as both diagnostic test and treatment, with a substantial response confirming the syndrome and guiding ongoing dosing. The reason for urgency is malignant catatonia, in which fever, autonomic instability and rigidity supervene with a mortality that approaches that of untreated neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and which requires electroconvulsive therapy without delay.
key_points: Catatonia most commonly complicates mood disorders rather than schizophrenia
Waxy flexibility, gegenhalten, mutism, negativism and echolalia are the defining motor signs
The benzodiazepine challenge is simultaneously diagnostic and therapeutic
Antipsychotics may precipitate malignant catatonia and are withheld until it resolves
Electroconvulsive therapy is definitive when the challenge fails or malignant features appear
explanation.pearls: A raised creatine kinase in a catatonic patient signals sustained isometric muscle activity and impending rhabdomyolysis, so it warrants intravenous fluids and a shift towards electroconvulsive therapy rather than a further week of benzodiazepine titration.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: Acute confusional state arising on a background of established dementia in a residential setting
stem:
You are the general practitioner called urgently to a residential aged care facility for an 81-year-old man with moderate vascular dementia who has become agitated overnight, trying to climb over the bed rails and shouting at staff that there are people in his room.

His baseline is that he needs help with dressing, knows the staff by sight and has never previously been aggressive or seen things that are not there. Staff report that over the past two days he has been drowsy in the afternoons but wide awake and frightened at night, and that his attention wanders mid-sentence in a way it did not last week. He fell in the bathroom four days ago and struck his hip, and was started on regular oxycodone the following day. His last bowel action was five days ago. The nurse asks you to chart regular risperidone for the behaviour.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104/min, blood pressure 116/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 94% on room air, temperature 37.4 C
data_table.Examination: Inattentive and unable to recite the months backwards past October, fluctuating alertness, distended non-tender abdomen with no bowel sounds heard over one minute, bladder percussible to the umbilicus, no focal neurology, no meningism
data_table.Investigations: Point of care blood glucose 6.8 mmol/L (4.0-7.8), oxygen saturation 94% on room air, no bloods yet taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Prescribe an as-required benzodiazepine overnight and arrange blood tests in the morning
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines worsen and prolong delirium in older people other than in alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, and they increase falls in a man already trying to climb over bed rails. Delaying investigation overnight also delays treatment of the retention and constipation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Chart regular risperidone as requested and reassess the agitation in the morning as planned
options.rationale: Antipsychotics do not shorten delirium or improve outcomes and are reserved for severe distress or danger when non-pharmacological measures have failed, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Charting a regular dose first treats the staff's request rather than the patient's illness. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard

options.text: Investigate and treat the precipitants, beginning with bladder drainage and a medication review
options.rationale: Acute onset with fluctuating course, inattention and altered consciousness on a dementia background defines delirium, and three precipitants are already visible in urinary retention, constipation and newly started opioid. Treating the causes resolves the delirium, whereas sedating him leaves every cause untouched and adds to the confusion. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard

options.text: Attribute the change to progression of his dementia and arrange a family meeting about his care needs
options.rationale: Dementia progresses over months and does not produce a two day change in attention and alertness, and this is the misattribution that makes delirium superimposed on dementia the most frequently missed presentation in aged care. Visual hallucinations that are new to a man with vascular dementia are a further pointer away from simple progression. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the brain to exclude a subdural haematoma from his recent fall
options.rationale: A fall four days ago in an older man does make subdural haemorrhage worth considering, and imaging should follow if he does not improve as the identified precipitants are corrected. Sending him to hospital for a scan before draining a palpable bladder addresses the least likely cause first. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard

explanation.summary: Delirium is an acute disturbance of attention and awareness that develops over hours to days, fluctuates across the day and is caused by an underlying medical condition, medication or substance. Dementia is the single strongest predisposing factor, which means the two coexist constantly, and delirium superimposed on dementia is both the commonest and the most frequently missed presentation because the baseline is already abnormal. The discriminator is the time course and the change in attention: dementia declines over months with preserved alertness, while delirium changes over days with impaired attention and a fluctuating conscious level. In a frail older person the precipitant is usually multiple and mundane, with urinary retention, constipation, infection, dehydration, pain and newly added medication accounting for most cases, and in Australia the Delirium Clinical Care Standard makes identifying and treating those causes the central obligation rather than managing the behaviour it produces.
key_points: Delirium is defined by acute onset, fluctuation, inattention and altered consciousness
Dementia is the strongest predisposing factor, so a changed baseline is the key history
Common precipitants are retention, constipation, infection, dehydration, pain and new drugs
Antipsychotics do not shorten delirium and are reserved for severe distress or danger
Benzodiazepines worsen delirium except in alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal
explanation.pearls: Hypoactive delirium is more common than the hyperactive form and carries a worse prognosis, yet it generates no staff request for review, which is why a brief attention test such as reciting the months of the year backwards should be applied to any older person whose alertness has changed rather than only to those who are agitated.

sources.label: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Delirium Clinical Care Standard

subtopic_detail: Biopsy technique for a pigmented skin lesion where melanoma is the clinical concern
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 52-year-old man who has noticed that a mole on his upper back has darkened and enlarged over the past five months. His wife says it looks different from his others.

He has fair skin that burns easily, worked outdoors for two decades and had a basal cell carcinoma excised from his nose four years ago. The lesion is 9 mm across with an irregular notched border, two shades of brown and a small black area at one edge. Dermoscopy shows an atypical pigment network with irregular streaks at the periphery. There is no ulceration and no palpable axillary lymphadenopathy.

data_table.Examination: 9 mm pigmented lesion on the upper back with border irregularity and colour variegation, no ulceration, no satellite lesions, no palpable axillary or cervical lymphadenopathy, numerous solar keratoses on the forearms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate way to obtain a tissue diagnosis?

options.text: Serial dermoscopic photography of the lesion with planned review in three months time
options.rationale: Short term sequential imaging is a legitimate tool for flat equivocal lesions without dermoscopic features of melanoma, allowing change to be detected over months. A lesion already showing an atypical network with irregular streaks and a documented history of growth has met the threshold for excision. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Shave biopsy of the raised component with diathermy to the base of the pigmented lesion
options.rationale: A shave transects the lesion at an arbitrary depth and destroys the deep margin with diathermy, making thickness unmeasurable. The near-pair distinction from the correct approach is that both remove tissue, but only full thickness excision preserves the depth the pathologist must report. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Partial punch biopsy taken from the most darkly pigmented area of the pigmented lesion
options.rationale: Sampling part of a lesion risks missing the deepest focus and therefore under-reporting Breslow thickness, which misdirects every subsequent management decision. Partial biopsy is acceptable only for very large lesions or sites such as the face where complete excision is not initially feasible. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Complete excision biopsy of the whole lesion with a two millimetre peripheral margin
options.rationale: Excisional biopsy including the full depth of the lesion allows the pathologist to measure Breslow thickness accurately, which is the single most important determinant of staging, definitive margins and whether sentinel node biopsy is offered. A narrow 2 mm margin is used because definitive wider excision follows once the thickness is known. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Wide local excision with a one centimetre margin performed at the initial operation today
options.rationale: Definitive margins are determined by Breslow thickness, which is not yet known, so excising widely now may be both excessive for a thin lesion and inadequate for a thick one. Performing a wide excision first can also disrupt lymphatic drainage and compromise later sentinel node mapping. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Clinical Practice Guidelines

explanation.summary: Australia has among the highest melanoma incidence rates in the world, and the prognosis depends overwhelmingly on how deeply the tumour has invaded at the time of excision. Breslow thickness, measured in millimetres from the granular layer to the deepest tumour cell, drives the definitive excision margin, the decision about sentinel lymph node biopsy and the staging conversation, which is why the initial biopsy must deliver an intact full thickness specimen. Ulceration and mitotic rate add further prognostic information from the same specimen. Once the thickness is reported, definitive wide local excision follows with margins graded to thickness, ranging from 5 mm for melanoma in situ up to 2 cm for thicker tumours.
key_points: Excision biopsy with a 2 mm margin and full depth is the standard diagnostic procedure
Breslow thickness determines definitive margins, sentinel node biopsy and staging
Partial and shave biopsies risk under-staging by missing the deepest tumour
Definitive margins range from 5 mm for in situ disease to 2 cm for thick melanoma
Sequential dermoscopic imaging is only for equivocal flat lesions without melanoma features
explanation.pearls: Sentinel lymph node biopsy is discussed for melanoma of Breslow thickness above 1 mm, and for thinner lesions with ulceration, because it provides staging information that determines eligibility for adjuvant immunotherapy rather than because it improves melanoma specific survival on its own.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Clinical Practice Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Imaging the sacroiliac joints when pelvic radiographs are normal in suspected axial inflammatory back disease
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 26-year-old man with 14 months of lower back and buttock pain that wakes him in the second half of the night and forces him to get up and move around. He has more than an hour of stiffness each morning that eases with activity and worsens with rest.

His pain has not responded to paracetamol but improved noticeably during a two week course of a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug. He had an episode of a painful red eye with photophobia treated by an optometrist last year. Examination shows reduced lumbar flexion on the modified Schober test and tenderness over both buttocks with no neurological deficit and a negative straight leg raise. An anteroposterior pelvic radiograph is reported as normal.

data_table.Examination: Modified Schober test 3.5 cm, chest expansion 4 cm, tenderness over both sacroiliac regions, no neurological deficit in the lower limbs, straight leg raise negative bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 14 mg/L (<5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 28 mm/h (<15), full blood count within normal limits, anteroposterior pelvic radiograph reported as normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat plain radiography of the sacroiliac joints with dedicated oblique views in two years
options.rationale: Dedicated views add little to a standard anteroposterior pelvic film, and waiting two years for structural change to appear delays treatment through the window in which it best preserves function. Radiographic progression is the natural history the treatment aims to prevent. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

options.text: Human leucocyte antigen B27 testing used on its own to confirm or exclude the diagnosis
options.rationale: This marker is useful as one element within a classification framework and raises the probability substantially in the right clinical context, but around 8% of the Australian population carries it and most carriers never develop disease. It cannot confirm the diagnosis alone and a negative result does not exclude it. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

options.text: Computed tomography of the sacroiliac joints to assess for erosion and joint space narrowing
options.rationale: Computed tomography shows established structural damage better than plain films but is insensitive to the active inflammation that precedes it, and it delivers a substantial pelvic radiation dose to a young man. It detects the same late changes the radiograph is waiting for. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the sacroiliac joints including fat suppressed sequences
options.rationale: Radiographic sacroiliitis takes years to develop, so a normal plain film in a young man with inflammatory back pain does not exclude the diagnosis and instead defines the non-radiographic form of the disease. Fat suppressed sequences demonstrate bone marrow oedema in the subchondral bone, which is the imaging criterion used for diagnosis. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine to look for disc protrusion and nerve root compression
options.rationale: Lumbar spine imaging investigates mechanical and discogenic pain, which characteristically worsens with activity and improves with rest, the opposite of his pattern. It also images the wrong joints, since the disease begins at the sacroiliac joints. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

explanation.summary: Inflammatory back pain is defined by a cluster of features that together separate it from the far more common mechanical causes: onset before 45 years, insidious onset, duration beyond three months, morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes, improvement with exercise but not with rest, and night pain that wakes the patient in the second half of the night. Recognising it matters because the average delay to diagnosis of axial spondyloarthritis has historically been measured in years, during which irreversible structural change accumulates. The disease is now understood as a spectrum, with non-radiographic disease at one end and ankylosing spondylitis with established radiographic sacroiliitis at the other, and magnetic resonance imaging is what makes the earlier end visible. Extra-articular features including acute anterior uveitis, psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease frequently accompany it and are often the clue that reframes a long history of back pain.
key_points: Inflammatory back pain improves with exercise, worsens with rest and wakes the patient at night
Plain radiographic sacroiliitis takes years to appear and its absence does not exclude disease
Magnetic resonance imaging with fat suppression shows active subchondral bone marrow oedema
Human leucocyte antigen B27 supports but never establishes the diagnosis
Acute anterior uveitis, psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease are associated features
explanation.pearls: Acute anterior uveitis affects up to 40% of people with axial spondyloarthritis and is typically unilateral, painful and recurrent, so a young adult presenting to an optometrist with a red painful photophobic eye and a history of chronic back pain should be asked directly about night pain and morning stiffness.

subtopic_detail: Medical rather than surgical first line therapy for a large prolactin secreting pituitary tumour
stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar seeing a 38-year-old man referred with two years of reduced libido and erectile dysfunction, and six months of bumping into door frames on his left side.

He takes no medication, has no chest pain and has never had a head injury. Formal perimetry confirms a bitemporal hemianopia denser superiorly. Serum prolactin measured on two occasions is 8400 milliunits/L and 8100 milliunits/L (85-500), with testosterone low, luteinising hormone and follicle stimulating hormone low, and thyroid function and early morning cortisol within normal limits. Magnetic resonance imaging shows a 24 mm pituitary lesion with suprasellar extension abutting the optic chiasm and no haemorrhage.

data_table.Examination: Bitemporal hemianopia on confrontation and formal perimetry, no ophthalmoplegia, visual acuity 6/6 bilaterally, no galactorrhoea, reduced body hair
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 8400 and 8100 milliunits/L (85-500), testosterone low, luteinising hormone and follicle stimulating hormone low, thyroid function and 8 am cortisol within normal limits, magnetic resonance imaging shows a 24 mm sellar mass with suprasellar extension

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Oral cabergoline titrated with serial prolactin measurement and repeat visual field testing
options.rationale: Prolactin secreting tumours are the one pituitary macroadenoma treated medically first, because dopamine agonists shrink them dramatically and normalise prolactin in the great majority, often improving visual fields within days to weeks. Cabergoline is preferred over bromocriptine for greater efficacy and better tolerability. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Hyperprolactinaemia)

options.text: Testosterone replacement therapy to correct his hypogonadal symptoms while monitoring the tumour
options.rationale: His hypogonadism is secondary to prolactin suppressing gonadotrophin releasing hormone pulsatility, so lowering prolactin restores the axis without exogenous hormone. Replacing testosterone alone leaves the tumour compressing his chiasm. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Hyperprolactinaemia)

options.text: Urgent transsphenoidal surgical debulking of the tumour to decompress the optic chiasm
options.rationale: Chiasmal compression would mandate urgent surgery for almost any other pituitary tumour, but here the mass usually shrinks faster with a tablet than it could be safely resected. Surgery is reserved for dopamine agonist resistance or intolerance, apoplexy, or progressive visual loss despite medical therapy. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Hyperprolactinaemia)

options.text: Stereotactic radiotherapy to the pituitary fossa with endocrine review every three months
options.rationale: Radiotherapy works slowly over years, carries a high long term rate of hypopituitarism and cannot relieve chiasmal compression in a useful timeframe. It is a third line option for tumours resistant to both medical and surgical treatment. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Hyperprolactinaemia)

options.text: Observation with repeat imaging and prolactin measurement in six months before any treatment
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is an option only for a small asymptomatic microadenoma with normal visual fields in a man not seeking fertility. Observing established chiasmal compression risks permanent visual loss. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Hyperprolactinaemia)

explanation.summary: Prolactinomas are the commonest functioning pituitary tumour and present differently by sex: women usually present early with amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea from a microadenoma, while men typically present late with hypogonadism and mass effect from a macroadenoma, because the endocrine symptoms are insidious and easily attributed to other causes. Before attributing a raised prolactin to a tumour it is essential to exclude the far commoner alternatives, which are pregnancy, hypothyroidism, renal failure, chest wall stimulation, stress and above all drugs such as antipsychotics, metoclopramide and some antidepressants. The magnitude of elevation is informative, since a level in the thousands with a macroadenoma indicates a prolactin secreting tumour, whereas a modest rise with a large sellar mass suggests stalk compression from a non-functioning tumour interrupting dopamine delivery. That distinction changes management completely, because stalk effect requires surgery while a prolactinoma responds to a dopamine agonist.
key_points: Prolactinomas are the only pituitary macroadenoma treated medically before surgically
Cabergoline is preferred to bromocriptine for efficacy and tolerability
Exclude pregnancy, hypothyroidism, renal failure and drug causes before diagnosing a tumour
Modest hyperprolactinaemia with a large mass suggests stalk compression rather than a prolactinoma
Surgery is reserved for resistance, intolerance, apoplexy or progressive visual loss
explanation.pearls: A very large prolactinoma can produce a falsely normal prolactin through the hook effect, in which massive antigen excess saturates both antibodies in the immunoassay, so a big sellar mass with an unexpectedly modest prolactin should be retested on a 1 in 100 dilution before it is called non-functioning.

subtopic_detail: Choosing a topical regimen for stable chronic plaque disease on extensor surfaces
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 41-year-old woman with a two year history of scaly patches on both elbows and knees that itch mildly and flake onto her clothes. She has tried an over the counter moisturiser and 1% hydrocortisone with minimal improvement.

She has no joint pain, no nail changes and no scalp involvement, and she takes no regular medication. Examination shows four well demarcated salmon pink plaques with thick silvery scale over both elbows and both knees, together involving around 4% of her body surface area. There are no plaques in the flexures, on the face or in the genital region, and the rest of her skin is clear.

data_table.Examination: Four well demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale on both elbows and knees, approximately 4% body surface area, no nail pitting or onycholysis, no scalp or flexural involvement, no joint swelling or tenderness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Narrowband ultraviolet B phototherapy attending a dermatology unit three times each week
options.rationale: Phototherapy is effective for widespread disease that topical treatment cannot cover, and it requires repeated hospital attendance. For four localised plaques the treatment burden far exceeds what topical therapy would ask of her. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: A further trial of a mild topical corticosteroid applied twice daily for six to eight weeks
options.rationale: Mild preparations are appropriate for the face, flexures and genitalia where skin is thin, but they are insufficient for thick scaly plaques on extensor surfaces and have already failed. Repeating an inadequate potency simply extends the time she remains untreated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Oral methotrexate commenced weekly with folic acid and regular blood test monitoring
options.rationale: Systemic therapy is considered for extensive disease, usually above 10% body surface area, for significant functional or psychological impact, or for psoriatic arthritis, none of which is present. Committing her to weekly monitoring for four small plaques is disproportionate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Topical coal tar preparation applied nightly under occlusion with emollient during the day
options.rationale: Coal tar is effective and still used, particularly for scalp disease and in specialist settings, but it stains skin and clothing and smells strongly, so adherence is poor. It sits behind the corticosteroid and vitamin D analogue combination in the Australian sequence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: A potent topical corticosteroid combined with calcipotriol applied to the affected plaques
options.rationale: Combining a potent corticosteroid with a vitamin D analogue is first line for localised chronic plaque disease and outperforms either component alone, because the steroid addresses inflammation while calcipotriol normalises keratinocyte proliferation. Extensor surfaces tolerate potent preparations well, unlike the face and flexures. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Chronic plaque psoriasis is an immune mediated disease of accelerated keratinocyte turnover producing sharply demarcated erythematous plaques with adherent silvery scale on extensor surfaces, scalp, nails and the natal cleft. Treatment intensity is matched to the extent of disease and its impact, with topical therapy for limited disease, phototherapy for more widespread involvement, and systemic conventional or biologic agents for severe or arthropathic disease. Topical corticosteroid potency is selected by site rather than by preference, since thin skin on the face, flexures and genitalia is vulnerable to atrophy while thick plaques on elbows and knees need potent preparations to penetrate. Psoriasis also carries systemic associations that a skin-only consultation misses, including psoriatic arthritis in up to a third of patients, and increased cardiovascular and metabolic risk that warrants screening.
key_points: A potent corticosteroid with calcipotriol is first line for localised plaque disease
Topical corticosteroid potency is chosen by body site, not by disease severity alone
Systemic therapy is for extensive disease, major functional impact or psoriatic arthritis
Screen for psoriatic arthritis, which affects up to a third of people with psoriasis
Cardiovascular and metabolic risk is increased and should be assessed
explanation.pearls: Abrupt withdrawal of systemic corticosteroid in psoriasis can precipitate generalised pustular or erythrodermic disease, which is why oral prednisolone is avoided in psoriasis even when a patient with severe plaques requests something to clear it quickly.

subtopic_detail: Initial management of chronic widespread pain once inflammatory disease has been excluded
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 45-year-old woman with four years of aching in her neck, shoulders, lower back and both thighs, present most days. She wakes unrefreshed after eight hours in bed and describes difficulty concentrating and finding words.

Her symptoms worsen with stress and cold weather. There is no joint swelling, no morning stiffness beyond 15 minutes and no rash, weight loss or fever. Examination shows a full range of movement in all joints with no synovitis, normal power and normal reflexes, but widespread tenderness to light palpation over the trapezius, gluteal and thigh muscles. Full blood count, C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, creatine kinase, thyroid function and vitamin D are all within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: No synovitis in any joint, full range of movement, normal power and reflexes, widespread soft tissue tenderness to light palpation, no rash, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, creatine kinase, thyroid function and vitamin D all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: A graded aerobic exercise programme with education about the condition and sleep strategies
options.rationale: Graded aerobic exercise has the strongest and most consistent evidence of any intervention for this condition, improving pain, function and fatigue, and it is paired with explanation of the diagnosis because understanding central pain amplification reduces fear and improves engagement. Non-pharmacological management is first line in every major guideline. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: A slow release opioid analgesic titrated to effect with review of her pain scores monthly
options.rationale: Opioids are ineffective for this condition and cause harm through tolerance, opioid induced hyperalgesia, dependence and cognitive impairment that compounds her existing concentration difficulty. They are specifically recommended against. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: An antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor panel with rheumatology referral if abnormal
options.rationale: Serological testing without clinical features of connective tissue disease generates false positives, since a low titre antinuclear antibody is present in a substantial minority of healthy people. That result then drives further investigation and diagnostic uncertainty rather than resolving it. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Fibromyalgia)

options.text: A regular non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug with a proton pump inhibitor for gastric protection
options.rationale: These agents work on peripheral inflammation, which is absent here, and trials show no meaningful benefit in this condition. Long term use adds gastrointestinal, renal and cardiovascular risk without addressing central sensitisation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Referral for magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical and lumbar spine before treatment starts
options.rationale: Imaging in widespread pain without neurological signs or red flags commonly shows age related degenerative change that is unrelated to the symptoms. Attributing the pain to incidental findings leads to unnecessary procedures and reinforces a structural explanation that is not correct. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Fibromyalgia)

explanation.summary: Fibromyalgia is a disorder of central pain processing rather than of peripheral tissue damage, characterised by widespread pain lasting beyond three months together with fatigue, unrefreshing sleep and cognitive difficulty that patients often describe as brain fog. It is a positive clinical diagnosis made on the symptom pattern, not a diagnosis of exclusion, though a limited screen for inflammatory, metabolic and endocrine mimics is appropriate. Overinvestigation is actively harmful because incidental findings invite structural explanations and procedures that do not help. Management is built on education, graded exercise, sleep and psychological approaches, with medication playing a secondary role through agents that act centrally such as amitriptyline, duloxetine and pregabalin, while opioids and non-steroidal agents are ineffective.
key_points: Fibromyalgia reflects central sensitisation rather than peripheral inflammation
It is a positive clinical diagnosis, not one of exclusion after exhaustive testing
Graded aerobic exercise has the strongest evidence of any intervention
Opioids and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are ineffective and cause harm
Centrally acting agents such as amitriptyline and duloxetine are adjuncts, not first line
explanation.pearls: Low dose amitriptyline at 10 to 25 mg taken two hours before bed is the most commonly used pharmacological adjunct in Australian practice, chosen for its effect on sleep continuity rather than its antidepressant action, and the dose used is far below the antidepressant range.

subtopic_detail: Immediate priority for rapidly progressive epidermal detachment after a recently started anticonvulsant
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the emergency department to see a 34-year-old woman with a three day history of fever, sore throat and painful eyes, followed today by a spreading rash that began on her trunk. She started lamotrigine 18 days ago for bipolar disorder.

She describes her skin as feeling like it is burning. Examination shows dusky macules with central blistering across her chest, back and proximal limbs, and gentle lateral pressure on unblistered skin at the edge of a lesion causes the epidermis to shear away. There are erosions on her lips, buccal mucosa and conjunctivae, and she cannot open her eyes fully. Around 12% of her body surface area is detached or detachable. She is haemodynamically stable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112/min, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 38.7 C
data_table.Examination: Dusky targetoid macules with central blistering over trunk and proximal limbs, positive epidermal shearing on lateral pressure, erosions of lips, buccal mucosa and conjunctivae, approximately 12% body surface area involved
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 11.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), eosinophils 0.2 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5), creatinine 96 micromol/L (45-90), bicarbonate 20 mmol/L (22-32), liver function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most important immediate action?

options.text: Commence broad spectrum intravenous antibiotics prophylactically and admit under the medical team
options.rationale: Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended because they select resistant organisms without reducing sepsis, and cultures with clinical surveillance guide treatment instead. Admitting to a general medical ward also denies her the nursing and wound care expertise the condition demands. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

options.text: Cease the causative drug immediately and transfer her urgently to a specialist burns unit
options.rationale: Early withdrawal of the culprit drug is the single intervention most consistently associated with reduced mortality, and management otherwise mirrors major burns care with fluid balance, temperature control, wound care, analgesia and infection surveillance. Mucosal and ocular involvement also requires early ophthalmology review to prevent permanent scarring and vision loss. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

options.text: Reduce the anticonvulsant dose and observe for 24 hours to see whether the rash stabilises
options.rationale: Dose reduction has no role because the reaction is immunologically mediated rather than dose dependent, and detachment progresses over days regardless. Observing for a day allows a potentially fatal reaction to extend. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

options.text: Commence high dose intravenous corticosteroid therapy and continue the anticonvulsant meanwhile
options.rationale: Systemic immunomodulation remains contested in this condition with no agent clearly established, and steroids may increase infection risk. Continuing the drug that is causing the reaction is the more serious half of this error. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

options.text: Arrange urgent skin biopsy for direct immunofluorescence before making any treatment decision
options.rationale: Biopsy is valuable to confirm full thickness epidermal necrosis and exclude autoimmune blistering disease, and it should be taken, but it takes time and the clinical picture already demands action. Waiting on histology before stopping the drug wastes the intervention that most affects survival. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

explanation.summary: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis are a single disease continuum of drug induced keratinocyte apoptosis, separated by the extent of epidermal detachment: below 10% of body surface area is Stevens-Johnson syndrome, above 30% is toxic epidermal necrolysis, and between the two is the overlap category. Anticonvulsants, allopurinol, sulfonamides, nevirapine and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs cause most cases, with onset typically 4 days to 4 weeks after the drug is started. Prodromal fever, sore throat and painful eyes precede the rash and are commonly mistaken for a viral illness, and mucosal involvement at two or more sites is close to universal. The SCORTEN score, calculated in the first 24 hours from age, heart rate, malignancy, body surface area detached, urea, bicarbonate and glucose, predicts mortality, which remains substantial in the more extensive form.
key_points: Stopping the culprit drug early is the intervention most associated with survival
Detachment below 10% is Stevens-Johnson syndrome and above 30% is toxic epidermal necrolysis
Management mirrors major burns care and belongs in a burns or intensive care unit
Early ophthalmology review prevents permanent ocular scarring and vision loss
Prophylactic antibiotics and routine systemic corticosteroids are not recommended
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine carries a particularly high risk of severe cutaneous reaction when titrated too quickly or combined with valproate, which inhibits its metabolism, so the Australian dose escalation schedule is halved when a patient is already taking valproate.

sources.label: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

subtopic_detail: Eosinophilic drug hypersensitivity with hepatic involvement six weeks after starting urate lowering therapy
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 61-year-old man with a widespread rash and fever for five days. He started allopurinol six weeks ago after a third episode of gout and takes perindopril for hypertension, unchanged for three years.

Examination shows a confluent morbilliform eruption covering around 60% of his body surface with marked facial oedema, particularly periorbitally. There is no epidermal detachment and no mucosal erosion, though his lips look dry. He has tender cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy. His creatinine has risen from a baseline of 88 to 174 micromol/L (60-110), alanine aminotransferase is 310 U/L (<40) and his eosinophil count is 2.4 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104/min, blood pressure 138/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 38.9 C
data_table.Examination: Confluent morbilliform eruption over approximately 60% body surface area, marked facial and periorbital oedema, tender cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy, no epidermal detachment, no mucosal erosions
data_table.Investigations: Eosinophils 2.4 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5), white cell count 14.6 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), alanine aminotransferase 310 U/L (<40), creatinine 174 micromol/L (60-110, baseline 88), atypical lymphocytes seen on blood film

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease the causative drug and transfer him urgently to a specialist burns unit for wound care
options.rationale: Burns unit transfer is the pathway for epidermal detachment with mucosal erosion, and his skin is intact with no shearing and no mucosal involvement. The organ dysfunction here is internal rather than a barrier failure. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

options.text: Cease the causative drug and manage with topical corticosteroid and oral antihistamine only
options.rationale: Topical treatment alone is appropriate for a simple morbilliform drug eruption without systemic features, which is the near-pair diagnosis here. The transaminitis, acute kidney injury and eosinophilia place this in a different category requiring systemic treatment. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

options.text: Cease the causative drug and commence systemic corticosteroid with prolonged tapering
options.rationale: Facial oedema, eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytes, lymphadenopathy and both hepatic and renal involvement six weeks after allopurinol describe drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, in which organ involvement justifies systemic corticosteroid. The taper must be slow over weeks to months because rapid withdrawal frequently causes relapse. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

options.text: Continue the causative drug at a reduced dose and add intravenous fluids for the kidney injury
options.rationale: The reaction is immunologically mediated and will progress on any dose, so reduction offers no protection while the kidney and liver injury worsens. Fluids support the kidney but do not address the cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Cease the antihypertensive as the likely cause and continue urate lowering therapy unchanged
options.rationale: A drug taken unchanged for three years is very unlikely to be responsible, whereas the latency of two to eight weeks fits the agent started six weeks ago precisely. Allopurinol is among the commonest causes of this syndrome worldwide. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

explanation.summary: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms is distinguished from other severe cutaneous adverse reactions by three features: a long latency of two to eight weeks after drug initiation, prominent facial oedema, and internal organ involvement accompanied by eosinophilia and atypical lymphocytes. The liver is affected most often, followed by the kidney, lung, heart and thyroid, and it is organ failure rather than the skin that causes death. Aromatic anticonvulsants, allopurinol, sulfasalazine, vancomycin, minocycline and dapsone account for most cases, and reactivation of human herpesvirus 6 and other herpesviruses is characteristically involved in the pathogenesis and helps explain the prolonged and relapsing course. Late autoimmune sequelae including thyroiditis and type 1 diabetes can emerge months after apparent recovery, so follow-up extends well beyond discharge.
key_points: Latency of two to eight weeks distinguishes this from other drug eruptions
Facial oedema, eosinophilia and atypical lymphocytes are characteristic
The liver is the most commonly involved internal organ, followed by the kidney
Systemic corticosteroid with a slow taper over weeks to months prevents relapse
