Late autoimmune sequelae such as thyroiditis warrant follow-up for months
explanation.pearls: Allopurinol hypersensitivity is strongly associated with the HLA-B*58:01 allele, which is why Australian practice starts allopurinol at 50 to 100 mg daily with slow upward titration against urate rather than beginning at a full dose, and why the risk is higher in patients with renal impairment.

subtopic_detail: First biochemical test when growth hormone excess is suspected from acral and facial change
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 47-year-old woman who has had three rings resized in two years and has gone up two shoe sizes. She mentions that her dentist commented her teeth have become more widely spaced.

She has been treated for carpal tunnel syndrome in both wrists, snores heavily and was diagnosed with hypertension and impaired glucose tolerance last year. She has noticed increased sweating and headaches. Examination shows a prominent brow and jaw, large fleshy hands, an enlarged tongue and skin tags on the neck. Her old photographs from ten years ago show visibly different facial contours. Visual fields are full to confrontation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78/min, blood pressure 154/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Frontal bossing, prognathism with interdental separation, macroglossia, spade-like hands, multiple skin tags, visual fields full to confrontation
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 6.6 mmol/L (3.0-5.4), HbA1c 45 mmol/mol (<42), electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: Which investigation should be requested first?

options.text: Overnight dexamethasone suppression testing with a morning cortisol measured the next day
options.rationale: This investigates cortisol excess, which also causes hypertension, glucose intolerance and skin changes, but produces central obesity, proximal myopathy, striae and easy bruising rather than acral enlargement and prognathism. The skeletal changes here point to a different hormone. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Acromegaly)

options.text: Random serum growth hormone level measured at the time of the consultation today
options.rationale: Pulsatile secretion means a healthy person can have an undetectable level between pulses and a high level during one, so a random measurement neither confirms nor excludes the diagnosis. This is the most common error in investigating suspected growth hormone excess. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Acromegaly)

options.text: Serum insulin-like growth factor 1 compared against an age and sex matched reference range
options.rationale: Growth hormone is secreted in pulses and has a short half life, so a single random level is uninterpretable, whereas insulin-like growth factor 1 is produced by the liver in proportion to integrated growth hormone exposure and is stable through the day. A raised age-adjusted level is the accepted screening test. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Acromegaly)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary with dedicated thin slices through the sella
options.rationale: Imaging localises the adenoma once biochemical excess is established, but pituitary incidentalomas are found in around 10% of scans in the general population. Imaging first risks attributing her symptoms to an unrelated incidental lesion. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Acromegaly)

options.text: Oral glucose tolerance test with serial growth hormone sampling over the following two hours
options.rationale: Failure of growth hormone to suppress after a glucose load is the confirmatory test and remains the reference standard, but it is performed after a raised insulin-like growth factor 1 has flagged the diagnosis. The near-pair distinction from the correct answer is screening versus confirmation. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Acromegaly)

explanation.summary: Acromegaly results from growth hormone excess, almost always from a pituitary somatotroph adenoma, and because the changes accrue over years the diagnosis is typically delayed by around a decade. Comparing current appearance with old photographs is one of the most useful clinical manoeuvres available. The clinical burden extends well beyond appearance, since growth hormone and insulin-like growth factor 1 excess drive hypertension, cardiomyopathy, obstructive sleep apnoea, insulin resistance, arthropathy, carpal tunnel syndrome and an increased incidence of colonic polyps, and untreated disease shortens life expectancy mainly through cardiovascular disease. Diagnosis follows a fixed sequence of screening with insulin-like growth factor 1, confirming with growth hormone suppression during an oral glucose tolerance test, then localising with magnetic resonance imaging. Transsphenoidal surgery is first line treatment, with somatostatin analogues, the growth hormone receptor antagonist pegvisomant, and radiotherapy for residual disease.
key_points: Insulin-like growth factor 1 is the screening test because it integrates pulsatile secretion
A random growth hormone level cannot confirm or exclude the diagnosis
Confirmation is failure of growth hormone suppression during an oral glucose tolerance test
Imaging follows biochemical confirmation because pituitary incidentalomas are common
Transsphenoidal surgery is first line, with medical therapy for residual disease
explanation.pearls: People with acromegaly have an increased risk of colorectal neoplasia, so Australian practice offers colonoscopy at diagnosis with ongoing surveillance intervals guided by the findings and by whether insulin-like growth factor 1 remains elevated after treatment.

subtopic_detail: Escalation after non-steroidal failure in purely axial disease without peripheral involvement
stem:
You are the rheumatology registrar reviewing a 31-year-old man with magnetic resonance imaging confirmed active sacroiliitis and 18 months of inflammatory back pain. He has completed sequential four week trials of two different non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs at maximum tolerated dose, with only partial relief.

He attends a structured physiotherapy programme twice weekly and has done so for six months. He has no peripheral joint swelling, no dactylitis, no enthesitis and no psoriasis or bowel symptoms. His Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Index remains high and he has reduced his work hours. C-reactive protein is 32 mg/L (<5) and screening for latent tuberculosis and hepatitis B is negative.

data_table.Examination: Restricted lumbar flexion, tenderness over both sacroiliac joints, no peripheral synovitis, no dactylitis, no enthesitis, no skin or nail psoriasis
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 32 mg/L (<5), magnetic resonance imaging shows bilateral active sacroiliitis with bone marrow oedema, interferon gamma release assay negative, hepatitis B and C serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next treatment?

options.text: Commence oral methotrexate weekly with folic acid supplementation and monthly blood monitoring
options.rationale: Conventional synthetic disease modifying drugs are ineffective for axial disease, a difference from rheumatoid arthritis that surprises many clinicians and reflects distinct underlying immunology. Methotrexate retains a role only for peripheral arthritis in this condition, which he does not have. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

options.text: Commence long term oral prednisolone at low dose with bone protection and gastric prophylaxis
options.rationale: Systemic corticosteroids are notably ineffective in axial disease, unlike in most other inflammatory arthritides, and long term use adds osteoporosis risk to a skeleton already vulnerable. Local corticosteroid injection into a sacroiliac joint is a different and sometimes useful intervention. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

options.text: Commence sulfasalazine titrated gradually with regular full blood count and liver function testing
options.rationale: Sulfasalazine has modest evidence for peripheral joint involvement in spondyloarthritis but none for axial disease. The near-pair distinction from the correct answer is that both are disease modifying, but only biologic therapy penetrates the axial skeleton's immunology. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

options.text: Continue the physiotherapy programme alone and reassess his disease activity in six months
options.rationale: Exercise and physiotherapy are the foundation of management and must continue alongside any drug, but they are not sufficient for persistently active disease with a C-reactive protein of 32 mg/L. Six months of ongoing inflammation permits further structural progression. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

options.text: Commence a tumour necrosis factor inhibitor after completing the required screening process
options.rationale: Biologic therapy is the recommended escalation for active axial disease that has failed at least two non-steroidal agents, and tumour necrosis factor inhibitors substantially improve symptoms, function and inflammatory markers. Latent tuberculosis and viral hepatitis screening has already been completed, which is the prerequisite for starting. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

explanation.summary: Axial spondyloarthritis behaves immunologically unlike rheumatoid arthritis, and the practical consequence is that the conventional synthetic disease modifying drugs which anchor rheumatoid treatment do essentially nothing for axial disease. The treatment ladder is therefore short: exercise and physiotherapy throughout, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs first line with at least two agents trialled for around four weeks each, then biologic therapy for persistently active disease. Tumour necrosis factor inhibitors and interleukin 17 inhibitors are both effective, and the choice between them is shaped by comorbidity, since inflammatory bowel disease and recurrent uveitis favour a monoclonal tumour necrosis factor inhibitor while interleukin 17 inhibition can worsen bowel disease. In Australia access is governed by Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme criteria requiring documented disease activity scores and failed non-steroidal trials, and all patients need latent tuberculosis and hepatitis screening before starting.
key_points: Methotrexate and sulfasalazine are ineffective for axial disease but may help peripheral arthritis
Systemic corticosteroids are ineffective in axial spondyloarthritis
Escalate to biologic therapy after two adequate non-steroidal trials with ongoing activity
Screen for latent tuberculosis and viral hepatitis before any biologic agent
Exercise and physiotherapy continue lifelong alongside drug treatment
explanation.pearls: Interleukin 17 inhibitors such as secukinumab can precipitate or worsen inflammatory bowel disease, so a patient with axial spondyloarthritis and coexisting Crohn disease should receive a monoclonal tumour necrosis factor inhibitor rather than an interleukin 17 agent or etanercept.

subtopic_detail: Reversing a factor Xa inhibitor for intracranial bleeding when the timing of the last dose is unknown
stem:
You are the medical registrar in a regional emergency department at 2 am. An 81-year-old woman has been brought in after being found confused on her bathroom floor by her son, who last spoke to her at 6 pm yesterday. She takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation, and her son cannot say whether she took her evening dose.

Her Glasgow Coma Scale score is 13 with a new left hemiparesis. Computed tomography of the brain shows a 32 mL right basal ganglia haematoma with early intraventricular extension and no underlying lesion. Her blood pressure is 192/104 mmHg. Point of care coagulation studies show a prothrombin time of 15 seconds and an activated partial thromboplastin time of 34 seconds, both near the upper limit of normal. Her creatinine is 142 micromol/L (45-90) and her weight is 58 kg. The hospital does not stock andexanet alfa.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88/min irregularly irregular, blood pressure 192/104 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.4 C
data_table.Examination: Glasgow Coma Scale 13 (E3 V4 M6), new left hemiparesis with left facial weakness, pupils equal and reactive, no external head wound
data_table.Investigations: Computed tomography brain shows 32 mL right basal ganglia haematoma with intraventricular extension; prothrombin time 15 s (11-14), activated partial thromboplastin time 34 s (25-35), platelets 214 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 142 micromol/L (45-90), haemoglobin 128 g/L (115-155)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate haemostatic management?

options.text: Withhold haemostatic therapy since the screening coagulation tests are close to normal
options.rationale: The prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time are insensitive to apixaban and can be normal at therapeutic drug concentrations, so they cannot be used to exclude anticoagulation. This is the central trap, because reassuring routine tests invite dangerous inaction. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Anticoagulant Reversal)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Anticoagulant Reversal

options.text: Give intravenous idarucizumab as the specific reversal agent for her direct oral anticoagulant
options.rationale: Idarucizumab is a monoclonal antibody fragment specific to dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor, and has no activity against factor Xa inhibitors. The near-pair distinction is the target enzyme: one class inhibits thrombin and the other inhibits factor Xa. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Anticoagulant Reversal)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Anticoagulant Reversal

options.text: Give intravenous vitamin K with fresh frozen plasma transfused according to her body weight
options.rationale: Vitamin K and plasma reverse warfarin by replacing vitamin K dependent factors, but apixaban directly inhibits factor Xa, so supplying more factor X in plasma at low concentration is ineffective. Plasma also carries volume overload risk in a frail 58 kg woman. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Anticoagulant Reversal)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Anticoagulant Reversal

options.text: Give activated charcoal by nasogastric tube and arrange urgent haemodialysis for drug clearance
options.rationale: Charcoal only helps within a few hours of ingestion, which cannot be established here, and apixaban is highly protein bound so dialysis removes very little. Dialysis is a genuine option for dabigatran, which is minimally protein bound, but not for this drug. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Anticoagulant Reversal)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Anticoagulant Reversal

options.text: Give prothrombin complex concentrate intravenously at a weight based dose without delay
options.rationale: With specific reversal unavailable, prothrombin complex concentrate is the recommended Australian alternative for life threatening bleeding on a factor Xa inhibitor and should be given immediately rather than awaiting drug level assays. Normal screening coagulation tests do not exclude a clinically significant apixaban effect, and her renal impairment prolongs elimination, so an unknown dose time must be assumed to mean she is anticoagulated. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Anticoagulant Reversal)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Anticoagulant Reversal

explanation.summary: Anticoagulant associated intracerebral haemorrhage carries a substantially higher risk of haematoma expansion and death than spontaneous bleeding, and expansion occurs predominantly within the first few hours, which is what makes reversal a time critical intervention rather than a considered one. The decisive point in this case is that routine coagulation assays cannot be used to decide whether a direct oral anticoagulant is active: the prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time are insensitive to apixaban in particular, and only a calibrated anti-factor Xa assay quantifies drug effect, which is rarely available overnight in a regional hospital. Reversal strategy follows the drug class, with idarucizumab for dabigatran, andexanet alfa for factor Xa inhibitors where stocked, and prothrombin complex concentrate as the Australian fallback. Alongside reversal, blood pressure lowering, neurosurgical consultation and seizure and airway management run concurrently rather than sequentially.
key_points: Prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time cannot exclude apixaban effect
Prothrombin complex concentrate is the fallback when andexanet alfa is unavailable
Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran only and has no effect on factor Xa inhibitors
Renal impairment prolongs direct oral anticoagulant elimination and raises drug levels
Haematoma expansion occurs early, so reversal precedes confirmatory drug assays
explanation.pearls: Dabigatran is around 35% protein bound and therefore dialysable, while apixaban and rivaroxaban exceed 85% protein binding and are not, which is why haemodialysis appears in the reversal pathway for one direct oral anticoagulant class and not the other.

sources.label: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Anticoagulant Reversal
Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

subtopic_detail: Urinary calcium excretion measurement before parathyroid surgery for familial hypercalcaemia
stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar seeing a 34-year-old man referred for parathyroidectomy. He was found to have a raised calcium on a routine check two years ago and repeat testing has shown persistently similar values since.

He has no bone pain, no renal colic, no polyuria, no constipation and no fractures, and he plays competitive squash. He takes no supplements, no thiazide and no lithium. A dual energy X-ray absorptiometry scan shows normal bone mineral density for age, and renal tract ultrasound shows no calculi and no nephrocalcinosis. His mother and one of his two sisters have also been told they have a high calcium and neither has had symptoms. A sestamibi scan reported no definite parathyroid adenoma.

data_table.Examination: No palpable neck mass, no bone tenderness, no proximal myopathy, hydration normal
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.78 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), parathyroid hormone 6.4 pmol/L (1.6-6.9), phosphate 0.94 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), creatinine 78 micromol/L (60-110), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 68 nmol/L (>50), sestamibi scan shows no definite adenoma, bone mineral density normal for age

lead_in: Which investigation should be performed before any surgical referral proceeds?

options.text: A serum angiotensin converting enzyme level with chest radiography to assess for granulomatous disease
options.rationale: Granulomatous disease raises calcium through unregulated conversion of vitamin D to its active form, which suppresses parathyroid hormone. It also would not explain the identical biochemistry in his mother and sister. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Hyperparathyroidism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Hyperparathyroidism

options.text: A repeat sestamibi parathyroid scan combined with four dimensional computed tomography imaging
options.rationale: Repeat localisation imaging assumes the diagnosis is primary hyperparathyroidism and merely asks where the gland is. A negative sestamibi in this context is a clue to reconsider the diagnosis rather than an indication to image harder. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Hyperparathyroidism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Hyperparathyroidism

options.text: A 24-hour urinary calcium creatinine clearance ratio calculated from paired blood and urine samples
options.rationale: A mildly raised calcium with an inappropriately unsuppressed parathyroid hormone occurs in both primary hyperparathyroidism and familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia, and the two are separated by urinary calcium handling, with a ratio below 0.01 indicating the familial condition. Distinguishing them is essential because parathyroidectomy does not cure the familial disorder and exposes the patient to an unnecessary operation. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Hyperparathyroidism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Hyperparathyroidism

options.text: A bone turnover marker panel with repeat bone densitometry performed in twelve months time
options.rationale: Bone markers and serial densitometry help decide whether asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism has met operative criteria, so they belong after the diagnosis is settled. His density is already normal, which does not discriminate between the two candidate diagnoses. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Hyperparathyroidism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Hyperparathyroidism

options.text: A serum parathyroid hormone related peptide level with computed tomography of the chest and abdomen
options.rationale: This pursues malignancy associated hypercalcaemia, in which parathyroid hormone is suppressed rather than unsuppressed, and which presents with a short history and higher calcium levels. His two year stable course with a normal parathyroid hormone points elsewhere. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Hyperparathyroidism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Hyperparathyroidism

explanation.summary: Hypercalcaemia with a parathyroid hormone that is not suppressed narrows the differential to parathyroid hormone dependent causes, and the important distinction within that group is between primary hyperparathyroidism and familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia. The latter is an autosomal dominant condition caused by an inactivating variant in the calcium sensing receptor gene, which resets the set point at which the parathyroid gland and the renal tubule perceive calcium as adequate, producing lifelong mild hypercalcaemia with avid renal calcium reabsorption and no end organ damage. The features that should raise suspicion are a young patient, an absence of renal stones and bone disease, a stable calcium over years, an affected first degree relative and a negative localisation scan. The calcium creatinine clearance ratio is the discriminating test, with values below 0.01 favouring the familial disorder and above 0.02 favouring primary hyperparathyroidism, and genetic testing confirming the diagnosis in the indeterminate zone.
key_points: Unsuppressed parathyroid hormone with hypercalcaemia indicates a parathyroid hormone dependent cause
Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia is autosomal dominant and caused by calcium sensing receptor variants
A calcium creatinine clearance ratio below 0.01 supports the familial condition
The familial condition causes no end organ damage and requires no surgery
A family history of asymptomatic hypercalcaemia and a negative localisation scan are key clues
explanation.pearls: Thiazide diuretics and lithium both reduce urinary calcium excretion and can push the calcium creatinine clearance ratio into the familial range, so either drug must be stopped for several weeks before the ratio is measured or the result will be uninterpretable.

subtopic_detail: New central nervous system white matter symptoms arising during biologic therapy for inflammatory arthritis
stem:
You are the rheumatology registrar reviewing a 38-year-old woman who has been taking adalimumab for 14 months for seropositive rheumatoid arthritis, with her joints in sustained remission.

For the past three weeks she has had blurred vision in the right eye with pain on eye movement, and she has noticed a band of numbness across her trunk below the ribs. She is afebrile with no headache, no rash and no recent infection. Examination shows reduced visual acuity of 6/18 in the right eye with a right relative afferent pupillary defect and normal fundi, brisk lower limb reflexes and extensor plantar responses. C-reactive protein is 3 mg/L and her full blood count is normal. Her interferon gamma release assay was negative before treatment and she has had no new travel or exposure.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 C
data_table.Examination: Right visual acuity 6/18 with relative afferent pupillary defect and normal fundoscopy, sensory level at T8, brisk lower limb reflexes with extensor plantar responses, no joint synovitis, no meningism
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 3 mg/L (<5), full blood count within normal limits, interferon gamma release assay negative before commencing treatment

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Attribute the findings to rheumatoid vasculitis and increase immunosuppression with cyclophosphamide
options.rationale: Rheumatoid vasculitis occurs in poorly controlled longstanding seropositive disease with high inflammatory markers, nodules and mononeuritis multiplex, whereas her arthritis is in remission with a C-reactive protein of 3 mg/L. Escalating immunosuppression for a misdiagnosed cause would expose her to substantial toxicity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Cease the biologic agent and arrange urgent neurology review with magnetic resonance imaging
options.rationale: Optic neuritis with a sensory level and upper motor neuron signs describes central demyelination, a recognised class adverse effect of tumour necrosis factor inhibitors that can unmask or precipitate a demyelinating illness. The drug is stopped permanently and the class avoided in future, while imaging of brain and spinal cord characterises the lesions. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Biologic Therapy Safety)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Biologic Therapy Safety

options.text: Continue the biologic agent and treat the episode with high dose intravenous methylprednisolone
options.rationale: Corticosteroid will shorten the acute attack and is part of the treatment, but continuing the drug that precipitated it leaves the cause in place and risks further demyelinating events. The class is contraindicated once this has occurred. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Biologic Therapy Safety)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Biologic Therapy Safety

options.text: Switch to a different tumour necrosis factor inhibitor and arrange neurology review as an outpatient
options.rationale: Demyelination is a class effect rather than a property of one molecule, so switching within the class reproduces the risk. The near-pair distinction from the correct answer is class avoidance versus agent substitution, which matters far more here than for infection related switching. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Biologic Therapy Safety)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Biologic Therapy Safety

options.text: Investigate for opportunistic central nervous system infection and commence empirical antimicrobials
options.rationale: Biologic therapy does raise the risk of tuberculosis and other opportunistic infection, so infection deserves consideration, but she is afebrile with a normal C-reactive protein, a negative pre-treatment screening test and a three week progressive course. The clinical syndrome localises to two separate white matter sites rather than to a mass or meningitic process. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Biologic Therapy Safety)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Biologic Therapy Safety

explanation.summary: Tumour necrosis factor inhibitors are among the most effective drugs in rheumatology, and their safety profile is dominated by infection risk, which is what most monitoring is built around. Central and peripheral demyelination is a less common but clinically decisive adverse effect, and it is counterintuitive because tumour necrosis factor blockade was originally trialled as a treatment for multiple sclerosis and made the disease worse. The practical consequences are twofold: a personal or family history of demyelinating disease is a contraindication to starting this class, and a new demyelinating event during treatment means permanent cessation and class avoidance rather than a switch within the class. Recognising the syndrome depends on localising the lesions clinically, and here optic neuritis with a thoracic sensory level demonstrates disease at two separate sites in the central nervous system. Alternative biologic classes with different mechanisms remain available for her arthritis once the neurological situation is characterised.
key_points: Demyelination is a class adverse effect of tumour necrosis factor inhibitors, not agent specific
A personal or family history of demyelinating disease contraindicates starting this class
A new demyelinating event means permanent cessation and avoidance of the whole class
Optic neuritis presents with pain on eye movement and a relative afferent pupillary defect
Alternative biologic classes with different mechanisms can be used for the arthritis
explanation.pearls: A relative afferent pupillary defect with normal fundi is the classic sign of retrobulbar optic neuritis and is elicited by the swinging torch test, in which the affected pupil paradoxically dilates as the light swings onto it because its afferent signal is weaker than the consensual one.
